0.title: Jesus Is Better: The Letter to the Hebrews
0.overview:
Who wrote the Letter to the Hebrews? The honest answer is: we do not know. Origen, the great third-century scholar who knew the church’s tradition better than almost anyone, concluded that only God knows who wrote it. Paul has been suggested — the theology runs as deep as any of his letters — but the literary style is far more polished and rhetorical than anything Paul wrote. Apollos, Barnabas, Priscilla, Luke — all have been proposed. In the end the mystery serves the text: Hebrews forces us to attend not to the human messenger but to the divine subject. The letter is about Jesus, and everything else in it orbits that sun.

The recipients were Jewish Christians — almost certainly a specific congregation, possibly in Rome (see 13:24, “those from Italy send you greetings”) — under intense pressure. Some had already suffered public shame, imprisonment, and the plundering of their property (10:32–34). Exhausted and frightened, they were tempted to drift back toward the synagogue, toward the familiar world of Temple sacrifice and priestly ritual. The writer’s response is not to demand more willpower but to open their eyes: you cannot go back, because going back is going backward — from substance to shadow, from fulfillment to promise, from Christ to the types that pointed toward him.

When was it written? Almost certainly before AD 70. The writer speaks of the priests and sacrifices as still going on (8:4; 10:1–3), and a letter arguing that the old system was passing away would hardly have left out the destruction of the temple if it had already happened. Timothy is alive and recently released (13:23). A date in the 60s fits best, and it matters: the readers were being drawn back to a temple that was still standing, and within a few years it would be gone.

Hebrews is structured as a “word of exhortation” (13:22) — a synagogue sermon put into written form. It alternates deliberately between doctrinal exposition and pastoral warning. The five great warning passages (2:1–4; 3:7–4:13; 5:11–6:20; 10:26–39; 12:25–29) are not interruptions to the argument; they are the argument’s pastoral urgency breaking through. Each one follows the same logic: if the lesser covenant carried consequences for violation, how much more the greater? The warnings grow in intensity as the letter progresses.

The controlling word of the letter is “better” (Greek: kreitton), used thirteen times. Jesus is the better revelation (ch. 1), the better mediator (chs. 2–3), the better rest (ch. 4), the better priest (chs. 5–7), the better covenant (ch. 8), the better sacrifice (chs. 9–10), and the ground of better and enduring possessions (ch. 10). The heroes of faith in chapter 11 were all seeking “a better country” (11:16). The letter culminates in the vision of Mount Zion, “the city of the living God” (12:22), and the unshakeable kingdom that no earthly power can topple (12:28).

Read Hebrews as a sustained pastoral argument for the all-sufficiency of Jesus Christ. Every argument leads back to him; every exhortation is grounded in him. The great High Priest has passed through the heavens, has offered himself once for all, has sat down at the right hand of God, and now — this is the astonishing thing — he continues to intercede for us. He is the same yesterday, today, and forever (13:8). Whatever the pressure, whatever the temptation to settle for something less, Hebrews speaks with one voice: hold fast to Jesus. There is nothing better. There is no one better. He is enough.

1.title: The Majesty on High: God Has Spoken His Final Word
1.overview:
Hebrews opens with no greeting, only a thunderclap. In four verses the writer sketches the Son across all of history: heir, creator, radiance of God’s glory, exact imprint of his nature, upholder of all things, purifier of sins, enthroned. Then the pivot of the whole letter: “he sat down”. Priests stood because their work was never done. Jesus sat because his is finished.

The chapter then compares the Son with angels, through whom the law was given (Acts 7:53). Seven Old Testament texts show that no angel was ever called God’s Son, worshipped by angels, addressed as God, or invited to sit at God’s right hand. Reduce Jesus to a prophet or teacher, and the rest of Hebrews collapses. This chapter will not allow it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — God Has Spoken by His Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hebrews opens without a greeting, like a sermon, which is what its author calls it (13:22). In the past God spoke through the prophets in fragments and in many different ways; now, at the climax of history, he has spoken in a Son. This Son is heir of everything and the one through whom God made the universe. He shines with God’s own glory, bears the exact imprint of his being, and sustains all things by his powerful word. Having made purification for sins, he took his seat at God’s right hand, and so ranks far above the angels, just as the name he has inherited is greater than theirs.
verseByVerse.theology:
Radiance and Imprint

God has not changed speaker; he has spoken finally, in a Son. Verse 3 holds together what the church later had to defend: the Son is one with the Father in nature and distinct from him in person — and, having made purification for sins, he sat down.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Jewish Christians under pressure were thinking of going back to what was partial.

Now: The way out of an old attachment is not to call it worthless but to see what it was pointing at.

verseByVerse.quote: Long ago, at many times and in many ways, God spoke to our fathers by the prophets,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Long ago, at many times and in many ways, God spoke to our fathers by the prophets,

Meaning first. Hebrews 1 opens the letter with a magnificent statement of who Jesus is. God, who spoke in many partial ways through the prophets, has now spoken his final word in his Son (vv. 1–2). The Son is described in seven great claims: heir of all things, agent of creation, radiance of God’s glory, exact imprint of his being, sustainer of the universe, the one who made purification for sins, and the one now seated at God’s right hand (vv. 2–3). He is therefore far greater than the angels (v. 4). The rest of the chapter proves this from seven Old Testament quotations (vv. 5–14): God calls the Son his Son, as he never called an angel; the angels are commanded to worship him; angels are servants, like wind and fire, but the Son is addressed as God, with an eternal throne; he is the Lord who made the earth and heavens and will outlast them; and he alone is invited to sit at God’s right hand, while the angels are ministering spirits sent to serve those who will inherit salvation. The chapter sets the theme of the whole letter: Jesus is better, and so to turn from him would be to turn from God’s final word.

The setting. The author of Hebrews is not named; Paul, Barnabas, Apollos, Luke, Priscilla and others have been suggested. The early church was divided: the Eastern church generally attributed it to Paul, while the Western church long doubted it. Origen, in the third century, famously said that only God knows who wrote it. The style and vocabulary are unlike Paul’s, and the author says he received the gospel from those who heard the Lord (2:3), which Paul insisted he did not (Galatians 1:12). Apollos, an eloquent Alexandrian Jew mighty in the Scriptures (Acts 18:24), fits the style well. Whoever the author was, he was a close associate of Timothy (13:23), and the church received the letter as Scripture. The readers were Jewish Christians, probably in or near Rome (13:24), written to before the destruction of the temple in AD 70, since the sacrifices are spoken of as still continuing (8:4; 10:1–2). They had suffered persecution (10:32–34), were tempted to drift back to Judaism to avoid further suffering, and had grown spiritually sluggish (5:11–14). The author writes a word of exhortation (13:22), really a sermon, showing that Christ is better than angels, Moses, Joshua, Aaron, the old covenant and its sacrifices, and calling them to hold fast.

A letter with no greeting. Every other letter in the New Testament begins the same way: a name, an address, grace and peace. Hebrews has none of it. It opens like a sermon, and that is almost certainly what it is: the writer calls it a word of exhortation at the end (13:22), the same phrase used of the address invited in the synagogue at Pisidian Antioch (Acts 13:15). He does not introduce himself, because he does not intend to be the subject. The first word of substance is God, and the first thing said about God is that he spoke.

Long ago, at many times and in many ways. The opening words in Greek are a piece of deliberate music: polymerōs kai polytropōs, a run of p-sounds that tells you at once that this writer could write, and intends to be listened to. But the two words are not decoration. Polymerōs means in many parts, piece by piece: a law here, a psalm there, a prophecy centuries later. Polytropōs means in many manners: a voice from a burning bush, a dream, a vision, a still small voice, a prophet told to marry an unfaithful wife and live the sermon in his own home. “Long ago” (palai) covers the whole stretch of Old Testament revelation, more than a thousand years of it. What both words describe is revelation that is real and incomplete. Not false: God genuinely spoke, and the writer will quote those Scriptures as authoritative on every page of this letter. But fragmentary, arriving in instalments, with no single prophet ever holding the whole.

God spoke to our fathers by the prophets. The God of the Bible is a speaking God (Isaiah 55:11). The idols of the nations had mouths and could not speak (Psalm 115:5); the living God broke the silence of the universe and addressed creatures he had made. “By the prophets” (literally in the prophets) means through Moses, David and all the Old Testament writers, men carried along by the Holy Spirit (2 Peter 1:21), so that what they said, God said. And “to our fathers” tells you who is being addressed: people who owned that history as family. This letter is written to Jewish Christians under pressure who are thinking of going back, and the writer does not begin by criticising what they are drawn to. He begins by affirming it. God really did speak there.

Partial, not wrong. Learn from his method. The argument of Hebrews is never that the old was wrong. It is that the old was partial, and that going back to a partial thing after the whole has arrived is the tragedy. You do not persuade someone out of an attachment by telling them it was worthless. You show them what it was pointing at. And notice the one constant across both verses: God spoke. He is the subject of this sentence and of the next. Whatever else divides the old covenant from the new, it is not a change of speaker.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Old Testament revelation was false or merely human. It was God’s word, true and authoritative. The contrast is not between false and true but between partial and complete, preparation and fulfilment.

Do I still need the Old Testament if God has spoken in his Son? Yes, very much. The Son did not replace the prophets; he fulfilled them, and you cannot understand the fulfilment without the promise. Jesus taught his disciples from Moses and all the Prophets the things concerning himself (Luke 24:27), and this very letter cannot say a sentence about Christ without quoting the Old Testament. The sacrifices, the priesthood, the tabernacle and the psalms are the vocabulary Hebrews uses to explain the cross. Read the Old Testament as a true word from God that is still speaking, and ask in each passage what it was preparing the world to see in Jesus.

In a sentence. In the past God spoke to our ancestors through the prophets, a little at a time and in many different ways,

On a Tuesday. If the Old Testament has become the part of your Bible you skip, choose one book this month, a psalm a day or a chapter of Genesis, and read it the way the writer of Hebrews did: as God himself speaking, in instalments, toward a Son. Before you read, ask him to show you where it is heading. After you read, write one line on what it tells you about the God who later came in Christ.

For worship. God did not have to speak at all. He could have left the world in the dark it chose, groping after him among idols with painted mouths. Instead he spoke, and kept speaking, through a thousand years of prophets who were mocked, ignored and killed, piece by piece and in every way a human heart could be reached. Every fragment was true, and every fragment was a promise. The God who would not stop talking to a people who would not stop running is the God who, at the end, sent the Word himself.
verseByVerse.note: The author of Hebrews is not named; Paul, Barnabas, Apollos and others have been suggested. It was written to Jewish Christians tempted to turn back from Christ, probably before the temple fell in AD 70.

verseByVerse.quote: but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son, whom he appointed the heir of all things, through whom also he created the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son, whom he appointed the heir of all things, through whom also he created the world.

But in these last days. The contrast is not between false and true but between then and now, between the instalments and the arrival. The prophets spoke of the last days as the time of the Messiah (Isaiah 2:2; Hosea 3:5). In the New Testament the whole stretch from Christ’s first coming to his return is the last days (Acts 2:17; 1 Corinthians 10:11). The writer means: the final era has started, and you are standing in it. Nothing that comes before the end will be more than this.

He has spoken to us by his Son. The Greek has no article: literally in Son (en huiō), which is almost impossible in English, but the force is clear. God spoke in the mode of a Son. The emphasis is on the kind of messenger. Previously the message came through servants who carried it; now it comes in a person who is it. The prophets had the word of God. The Son is the Word of God (John 1:1, 18). That is the difference the whole letter turns on. A prophet could be entirely right and still stand outside what he announced. Isaiah could foresee the suffering Servant without being him. Here the messenger and the message are the same, which is why there can be nothing after him. Not because God has run out of things to say, but because he has said himself.

Seven statements in a single arc. Then seven statements about the Son begin, running through verses 2 and 3 in a deliberate shape: heir, creator, radiance, imprint, sustainer, purifier, enthroned. They move from the end of history back to its beginning, up into the being of God, out into the running of the universe, down into the dirt of human sin, and back up to the throne. It is the whole story of Christ told in one sentence, and the first two come here.

Whom he appointed the heir of all things. “Heir” (klēronomos): in the ancient world the firstborn son inherited his father’s estate. Everything that exists is the Son’s inheritance, not part of it, all of it (Matthew 28:18). The word looks back to Psalm 2, which the writer will quote in three verses: ask of me, and I will make the nations your heritage (Psalm 2:8). Everything was made for him (Colossians 1:16), and everything will be summed up in him (Ephesians 1:10).

Through whom also he created the world. Here is the chronology that should stop a reader. The heir of all things is the one through whom all things were made (John 1:3; Colossians 1:16; 1 Corinthians 8:6). He did not inherit an estate somebody else built. He made it, and then received it back, so the inheritance is not a promotion but a homecoming. The whole letter’s argument about a Son who was humbled and then crowned is already in the sentence. And the word translated “world” is aiōnas, literally the ages. He made not merely the material universe but time itself, the whole run of history in which God spoke in many portions and many ways. The prophets lived inside a calendar the Son had made.

Where Christians differ: is revelation still ongoing? Some charismatic teaching expects ongoing prophetic revelation from God alongside Scripture; some liberal theology sees revelation as continuing through human experience. Verdict: God’s speaking in the Son is final. The apostles and their associates recorded and explained this revelation in the New Testament, and with them the canon closed (Jude 3; Revelation 22:18–19). God still illumines his word by his Spirit, applies it to our hearts, and guides us providentially, but he does not give new revelation equal to Scripture. Scripture alone is sufficient (2 Timothy 3:16–17).

What it does not mean. “Appointed heir” does not mean the Son was not always divine or that he earned his status. As eternal Son, he has always been Lord; as incarnate Son, having completed his work, he was appointed heir as the God-man.

If God’s word is final, how does he guide me today? Through the word he has already given, opened to you by his Spirit. He has not left you without direction; he has given you a complete Bible that is enough to make you wise for salvation and equip you for every good work (2 Timothy 3:15–17). Within what Scripture commands, he guides by wisdom, by the counsel of mature believers, by the ordinary providences of life, and by desires he has shaped in you. When an impression or a feeling comes, test it by the word and hold it loosely; never treat it as a voice from God that you must obey. The Son has spoken. To hear God speak today, open what he has said.

In a sentence. but in these final days he has spoken to us through one who is his Son, whom he has made heir of everything and through whom he made the universe.

On a Tuesday. Notice where you go first when you need to hear from God: a feeling, a sign, a favourite speaker, a verse plucked at random. Then try the harder and better road. Take a Gospel, read a passage slowly, and ask: what does this show me of the Son, and what does he say to me here? If God has said himself in Jesus, then the surest place to hear him on an ordinary weekday is in the pages where Jesus speaks and acts.

For worship. The one who made the ages entered them. The Son for whom the universe exists, who hung the stars and set the calendar running, came into his own estate as a baby in a borrowed stable and was treated by the tenants as an intruder. And the Father, at the end, gave it all back to him: every nation, every age, every thing. God has no word left that is greater than this one, because there is no one greater than his Son.

parallels.desc: I will make the nations your heritage

verseByVerse.quote: He is the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature, and he upholds the universe by the word of his power. After making purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high,
verseByVerse.commentary:
He is the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature, and he upholds the universe by the word of his power. After making purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high,

He is the radiance of the glory of God. Now come the two great words, and they are as high a statement about Christ as the New Testament contains. “He is” (ōn, being) is present tense: not what he became, but what he eternally is. “Radiance” (apaugasma) means the shining forth, the effulgence, the light that streams from a source. The picture is exact in a way that matters. The sun and its brightness are not two things. You cannot have the sun without the radiance, and there was never a moment when the sun existed and its light had not yet begun. The radiance is not a lesser substance the sun produced. It is the sun, reaching you. That is what the writer says the Son is to the Father. And “glory” (doxa) is the visible splendour of God’s being, the thing Moses begged to see and could only glimpse from behind (Exodus 33:18–23), the thing the disciples beheld in the Word made flesh (John 1:14), the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6).

And the exact imprint of his nature. Charaktēr, from which we get our word character, is the die used for stamping coins, and by extension the impression it leaves, every line of the original reproduced exactly in the metal. Not a likeness or an approximation: precise correspondence. “Nature” (hypostasis) here means essence, the very being of God. As a seal leaves its exact image in wax, so the Son is the exact representation of the Father’s being. To see him is to see the Father (John 14:9; Colossians 1:15). Later the church used hypostasis to mean person, but here it means being.

Both truths in one clause. Put the two images together and you have both truths the church later fought for at Nicaea. Radiance: he is not a second God, any more than light is a second sun. Imprint: he is genuinely distinct, as a stamped coin is distinct from the die. One in nature, distinct in person, and the writer says it in a single clause without a council’s vocabulary. Every heresy about Christ has had to cut one of these two words out of the verse.

And he upholds the universe by the word of his power. The verb (pherōn) does not mean holding a weight steady, as Atlas is pictured with the globe on his shoulders. It means carrying something along, bearing it forward toward an end. The Son is not propping creation up; he is conducting it somewhere. And it is present tense: continuously, now. He does it by the word of his power, his powerful word, by speaking. The same means by which the world was made is the means by which it continues (Colossians 1:17). If he fell silent, it would stop. Every atom in your body this morning exists because the Son has not stopped speaking it into being.

After making purification for sins. Then the sentence turns, and the turn is the whole gospel. The one who carries the universe stooped to deal with dirt. “Making purification” (katharismon poiēsamenos) is a completed act. In the Old Testament purification was made by blood (Leviticus 16:30), on the Day of Atonement, by a high priest who had to make it again the next year. Christ made purification by his own blood, once for all (9:12–14, 26). The Creator and Sustainer became the priest who cleanses sin, and the whole central argument of the letter is folded into these three Greek words.

He sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high. This is the detail the writer will return to and hammer in chapter 10. No priest in the tabernacle ever sat down. There were no chairs in it, because the work was never finished (10:11). A seated priest is a priest with nothing left to do. Christ sat down because his work of purification was complete (10:12). Everything Hebrews will argue about the finality of the sacrifice is already contained in two words about furniture. The right hand is the place of honour, authority and power (Psalm 110:1), and “the Majesty on high” is a reverent Jewish way of naming God without pronouncing his name.

Prophet, priest and king. These clauses are the seed of what later theology called Christ’s threefold office. He has spoken as the prophet (v. 2), made purification for sins as the priest, and sat down at the right hand as the king. Prophet, priest and king, the three anointed offices of Israel, all land on one man in a single sentence. In Israel the offices were kept apart: Aaron never wore a crown, and when King Uzziah went into the temple to burn incense he was struck with leprosy (2 Chronicles 26:16–21). The Son holds them all.

What it does not mean. “Radiance” and “imprint” do not mean the Son is a lesser copy or a separate god. He is of the same essence as the Father, fully God, yet a distinct person (John 1:1). Nor does “sat down” mean Christ is inactive; he reigns and intercedes (7:25). It means his atoning work is finished.

If he made purification once for all, why do I still feel dirty? Because feeling and fact are different things, and the conscience is slow to believe good news. The purification is finished whether or not you feel clean, because it rests on what Christ did, not on what you sense. When guilt returns over a sin you have already confessed, do not try to make purification again by punishing yourself or promising harder. Bring it to him, and remember that he is seated: there is nothing left to add. If a sin is new, confess it, and the same blood that cleansed you once cleanses you still (1 John 1:7–9). Feeling usually follows faith, slowly. Let the fact lead.

Does Jesus really hold my life together, down to the small things? Yes. If he upholds the universe by his word, there is nothing in it too small for him: the cells in your body, the timing of a phone call, the weather on the day of the funeral. That is not fatalism, because the one who holds it is not a force but a person, the same person who made purification for your sins. The hand that carries the stars is a pierced hand. You can trust the details of your life to someone who already gave himself for the whole of it.

In a sentence. The Son is the shining out of God’s glory and the exact expression of his being, and he keeps the whole universe going by his powerful word. After he had made cleansing for sins, he took his seat at the right hand of the Majesty in heaven,

On a Tuesday. When something in your life feels as though it is coming apart, say this verse aloud before you do anything else: he upholds the universe by the word of his power. Then bring the specific thing to him. And when an old sin comes back to accuse you, answer it with the other half: he made purification for sins and sat down. A seated Saviour is the end of the argument.

For worship. The light of God’s own glory, without beginning and without dimming, took a body that could be struck. The hands that carry the universe toward its end were nailed to wood, and the Word that holds every atom in place was silent before Pilate. He made purification not with the blood of bulls but with his own, and then he did what no priest in Israel had ever done. He sat down. The work is finished, the throne is occupied, and the one who sits on it is the radiance of God, who knows your name.

verseByVerse.quote: having become as much superior to angels as the name he has inherited is more excellent than theirs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
having become as much superior to angels as the name he has inherited is more excellent than theirs.

Having become as much superior to angels. The first question is why angels at all. Ten verses on their inferiority look like an odd priority to a modern reader, but not to the first one. In Jewish thought angels were the highest created beings and, crucially, the mediators of the law: Stephen says it was delivered by angels (Acts 7:53), and Paul says the same (Galatians 3:19), and this letter will say it at 2:2. So to ask whether the Son outranks angels is to ask whether the new word outranks the old one. It is not a question about celestial hierarchy. It is a question about which covenant to live under.

Having become. A word needing care. The Son did not become divine, and everything in verse 3 forbids reading it so. What he became was superior in office. As the eternal Son he was always above the angels; in his incarnation he was made for a little while lower than the angels (2:9); and by his death, resurrection and ascension, as the God-man, he was exalted far above them (Ephesians 1:20–21; Philippians 2:9). The becoming belongs to the incarnation and the enthronement, not to his nature. And “superior” (kreittōn, better) is the keyword of Hebrews, used thirteen times: a better hope, a better covenant, better promises, better sacrifices, a better possession, a better country, a better resurrection. This is its first appearance, and everything that follows is an unfolding of it.

As the name he has inherited is more excellent than theirs. In Scripture a name expresses character, status and identity. Which name? The next verse answers immediately, and it is the one thing no angel is ever called in this unique sense: Son. It may also include Lord, the name above every name (Philippians 2:9–11). And it is inherited (keklēronomēken, perfect tense: he inherited it and still holds it). That is family language again. A servant may be trusted with everything and inherits nothing; the name comes with the relationship.

A gap measured by a gap. Notice how the comparison is framed. Not superior to angels simply, but superior in the same proportion as the name is more excellent. The writer measures one gap by another, and since the distance between Son and servant is a difference in kind rather than degree, so is the other. The angels are not a little below Christ on the same ladder. They are on the other side of the line between Creator and creature.

The setting. Why compare Christ to angels? In Jewish thought, angels were highly honoured. They were believed to have mediated the giving of the law at Sinai (2:2; Acts 7:53; Galatians 3:19). Some Jews speculated about angels as great powers, and some may have seen Jesus as an angelic being. By showing that Christ is far superior to the angels who brought the old covenant, the author shows that the new covenant he brings is far superior too.

Proof by Scripture. This verse is the hinge into what follows. Having asserted the superiority, the writer now proves it, and not by argument. He will quote seven passages of the Old Testament in a row, on the assumption that his readers will accept a text as settling anything. That is a considerable compliment to pay a congregation, and it tells you what kind of people these were, and what kind of people a sermon can make.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ was once an angel, or a created being of a higher order. He created them (v. 2; Colossians 1:16). Nor does “became” mean he was not always divine. It refers to his exaltation as the incarnate Mediator.

Why does it matter to me that Jesus is greater than the angels? Because whatever you are tempted to put alongside him, it ranks below him. Few Christians today are tempted to worship angels, but many are drawn to something that feels more impressive, more immediate or more spiritual than plain trust in Christ: a powerful experience, a special teacher, a tradition, a technique for reaching God. The readers of Hebrews were tempted to go back to a system given through angels. The answer to every such pull is the same: nothing God has made is on the level of the Son who made it. If you have him, you are not missing anything higher.

In a sentence. and so he has become as much greater than the angels as the name he has inherited is greater than theirs.

On a Tuesday. Ask yourself what you reach for when Christ feels ordinary: a new teacher, a dramatic experience, a stricter set of rules, a spiritual high you once had. Name it. Then set it beside the seven claims of verses 2 and 3, one by one, and ask whether it made the world, holds it up, or cleansed you from sin. Nothing else will survive the comparison, and you will find your affection returning to the one who did.

For worship. The Son went lower than the angels so that we could be raised higher than we ever were. He laid aside the glory they had always watched him wear, took the name of a servant and the death of a criminal, and was given back the name above every name. The angels who once sang at his birth now cover their faces before his throne, and the one they worship calls those he redeemed his brothers.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–14 — Seven Texts, and Not One of Them About an Angel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The writer proves his point entirely from Scripture. No angel was told, “You are my Son.” The angels are told to worship the Son. Angels are made winds and flames; the Son is addressed, “Your throne, O God, is forever.” Of the Son it is said, “You, Lord, laid the foundation of the earth… you remain.” No angel was told, “Sit at my right hand.” Angels are servants sent to help those who will inherit salvation.
verseByVerse.theology:
Texts About God, Applied to Jesus

Scriptures addressed to God — Psalm 45 and Psalm 102 — are read as addressed to the Son, and the angels are commanded to worship him. A being the angels worship cannot be one of them.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Readers who had lost property and standing were told that earth and sky are the temporary things; the Son remains.

Now: The angels, far from rivals, are sent to serve those who will inherit salvation.

verseByVerse.quote: For to which of the angels did God ever say, “You are my Son, today I have begotten you”? Or again, “I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son”? And again, when he brings the firstborn into the world, he says, “Let all God’s angels worship him.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
For to which of the angels did God ever say, “You are my Son, today I have begotten you”? Or again, “I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son”? And again, when he brings the firstborn into the world, he says, “Let all God’s angels worship him.”

For to which of the angels did God ever say. The argument is conducted entirely by quotation, and the form of the question repays notice. It is rhetorical, expecting the answer none. The writer is not so much building a case as inviting his readers to search their own Scriptures and find the exception. There is not one.

You are my Son, today I have begotten you. The first citation is Psalm 2:7, a royal psalm in which God installs his King on Zion while the nations rage. It is a coronation psalm, spoken over a king of Israel on the day he took the throne, and “today” is the enthronement day, not a statement about origins. That matters, because the verse has been misused. It does not mean the Son began on a particular day; it means that on a particular day he was publicly installed. The New Testament applies it to Christ’s resurrection and exaltation, when he was declared the Son of God in power (Acts 13:33; Romans 1:4). His eternal sonship was openly proclaimed, and he was enthroned as the Messianic King.

I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son. The second is from God’s promise to David about his offspring (2 Samuel 7:14; 1 Chronicles 17:13). In its own setting it concerns Solomon, and the very next line of that passage speaks of disciplining him when he commits iniquity, which shows the promise always reached beyond the man in front of it. Solomon built the temple and ended in idolatry. No son of David ever exhausted the promise of a throne established for ever (2 Samuel 7:13, 16), and the writer takes it as pointing to the one who would.

But are angels not called sons of God? Yes, but always as a group. Job speaks of the sons of God presenting themselves before the LORD and shouting for joy at creation (Job 1:6; 38:7): the heavenly host, the members of God’s court. What God never said to any angel is what he says here to one person: you are my Son, my heir, my king enthroned. The plural title describes a class of creatures. The singular names the one through whom God made the world (v. 2). Believers too are called sons of God, but by adoption, through the Son who is Son by nature (Galatians 4:4–7).

And again, when he brings the firstborn into the world. “Firstborn” (prōtotokos) needs the same care as “begotten”. In Hebrew usage it is a title of rank, not chronology. God calls Israel his firstborn (Exodus 4:22), and David is made firstborn though he was the youngest of eight brothers (Psalm 89:27). It means the heir, the one with pre-eminence (Colossians 1:15, 18). “Brings into the world” may refer to his incarnation, when the angels praised God at his birth (Luke 2:13–14), or his resurrection, or, most likely, his return in glory: the word “again” may go with “brings”, so that it reads, when he brings the firstborn into the world again.

Let all God’s angels worship him. The words match the Greek Old Testament of Deuteronomy 32:43, which is longer than the Hebrew; a similar thought appears in Psalm 97:7. And the quotation is decisive for the argument, because it commands the angels to worship him. That settles the question absolutely. Angels are worshippers, and in Scripture they consistently refuse worship when it is offered to them: when John fell at an angel’s feet he was told to worship God (Revelation 19:10; 22:8–9). Only God may be worshipped (Matthew 4:10). The being the angels are commanded to worship cannot be one of them, and cannot be a creature at all, because the first commandment forbids it. So the writer has moved in two verses from Son, to heir, to an object of angelic worship, and he has done it entirely out of texts his readers already believed.

Textual note. The Dead Sea Scrolls contain a Hebrew text of Deuteronomy 32:43 that includes the line about the gods (or angels) bowing down, which supports the Greek translation used here as reflecting an ancient Hebrew form of the text.

What it does not mean. “Today I have begotten you” does not mean the Son was created or had a beginning. The church confesses him as eternally begotten of the Father, a relationship without beginning. Nor does “firstborn” mean first created (as Jehovah’s Witnesses argue); it denotes supremacy and inheritance.

What does eternally begotten mean? It means the Son’s relationship to the Father is that of a son, sharing his very nature, without ever having had a beginning. A human father exists before his son; the eternal Father never existed without his Son, any more than the sun existed before its light (v. 3). Begotten is not made: a man makes a table, but he begets a son, someone of his own kind. So the Nicene Creed says the Son is begotten, not made, of one being with the Father. You do not need to picture it to believe it. It simply guards the truth that the one who died for you is not a creature God sent, but God himself who came.

How do I answer someone who says Jesus is a created being? Start where this chapter starts: with what Scripture says to him and about him. He made all things (v. 2; John 1:3), so he cannot be one of the things made. Angels are commanded to worship him (v. 6), and worship belongs to God alone. He is addressed as God (v. 8) and as the LORD who laid the foundations of the earth (v. 10). Ask your friend to read the chapter with you, slowly, and to say what each verse claims. Be gentle and patient; most people who hold this view were taught it, and the Spirit uses the plain words of Scripture to open eyes.

In a sentence. God never said to any angel, You are my Son; today I have become your Father. Nor did he say of any angel, I will be his Father, and he will be my Son. And when he brings his firstborn into the world, he says, All God’s angels must worship him.

On a Tuesday. Next time you are in a service and the congregation sings to Christ, remember who else is singing. The highest beings in the universe have been commanded to worship the one you are addressing. Let that steady you in the ordinary moments too: when you pray to Jesus on the bus or at the sink, you are doing the very thing heaven does, and you are doing it to the right person.

For worship. The Father has one Son, and he loves to say so. He said it at the coronation of David’s line, he said it at the Jordan when the heavens opened, he said it on the mountain when the face of Jesus shone, and he said it by raising him from the dead. And when the Son came into the world, God turned to the whole host of heaven and commanded them to bow. They bowed at Bethlehem over a manger. They will bow again when he comes in glory. And the Son they worship is not ashamed to call us his brothers.
verseByVerse.note: The words of v. 6 match the Greek Old Testament of Deut 32:43, which is longer than the Hebrew.

verseByVerse.quote: Of the angels he says, “He makes his angels winds, and his ministers a flame of fire.” But of the Son he says, “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever, the scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Of the angels he says, “He makes his angels winds, and his ministers a flame of fire.” But of the Son he says, “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever, the scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions.”

Of the angels he says, He makes his angels winds, and his ministers a flame of fire. Now the contrast is drawn directly, and the writer sets two quotations side by side. The first is Psalm 104:4, following the Greek translation. The word for angels (angelous) means messengers, and the word for winds (pneumata) also means spirits. “Ministers” (leitourgous) are servants, those who perform public service. Wind and fire are impressive things, and they are also transient, changeable, and entirely at somebody else’s disposal. A flame is sent; it does not send itself. The point of the citation is the word makes: angels are things God made and uses as he wills, however glorious they are. Their very form and function change at his command.

But of the Son he says, Your throne, O God, is forever and ever. What follows is one of the most striking quotations in Scripture. It is Psalm 45:6–7, and Psalm 45 is a wedding song for an Israelite king. In its original setting the king is addressed, and addressed as God (ho theos, used as a direct address). Translators have wrestled with it for centuries, and some render it “your throne is God’s throne” to avoid the difficulty. But the writer of Hebrews read it as it stands, addressing the Son directly as God, and built his argument on it. In its first setting it was a breathtaking way to speak of a human king; its full meaning is realised only in the Messiah, who is truly God. It is one of the clearest statements of the Son’s deity in Scripture. And the throne is for ever and ever: his kingdom is eternal (2 Samuel 7:16; Daniel 7:14; Luke 1:33), against the changing winds and flames of the verse before.

Their own psalm. Set that beside the letter’s first readers. These are Jewish believers whose foundational confession is that the LORD our God is one. The writer is not smuggling divinity into the argument. He is showing them that their own Scriptures, in a psalm they had sung all their lives, address the Messiah as God and give him an everlasting throne. The confession that God is one is not denied by the Son. It is filled out by him.

The scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom. The sceptre (rhabdos) is the rod of rule, and uprightness (euthytēs) is straightness, justice. His rule is perfectly just (Isaiah 11:3–5). The reign is characterised morally before it is characterised in any other way. History has known many thrones and very few straight sceptres. This one has never bent.

You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness. This is Christ’s perfect moral character: he loved what is right and hated evil, perfectly, throughout his earthly life (4:15; 7:26). And note the pairing. Loving right and hating wrong are the same disposition seen from two sides. A man who genuinely loves one will hate the other, and an indifference to wickedness is not gentleness but a failure of love. Jesus could weep over Jerusalem and drive the traders from the temple in the same week, because the love and the hatred came from one heart.

Therefore God, your God, has anointed you. Two things are held together without embarrassment: the Son is addressed as God, and he has a God. That reflects the distinction of persons in the Trinity and the Son’s role as incarnate Mediator, who could say on resurrection morning, I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God (John 20:17). Hebrews states both halves in a single sentence without attempting to resolve the mystery. “Anointed” (echrisen) is the root of the word Christ: Messiah, Anointed One. Kings and priests were anointed with oil; Christ is the anointed King.

With the oil of gladness beyond your companions. The oil of gladness was used at festivals and coronations, a sign of joy, and it is worth carrying away. The anointing of this king is not solemn but joyful, and it is beyond his companions, more than anyone else in the room. His companions (metochoi, partners, sharers) may be other kings, or angels, or his people who share in his kingdom; the same word is used of believers at 3:1 and 3:14. Whatever else the exalted Christ is, Hebrews says he is the gladdest being in the universe. He endured the cross for the joy that was set before him (12:2), and now the joy is his.

What it does not mean. “God, your God” does not mean the Son is less than God. He is God the Son; in his mediatorial role as the God-man, he relates to the Father as his God. Nor does Psalm 104 deny the reality of angels; it describes their servant role.

Should a Christian hate anything? Yes: what Christ hates, which is wickedness, and above all our own. Hatred of evil is not a sin; indifference to it is. But the hatred of Christ is never contempt for people. He hated sin and ate with sinners. So hate the lie, the cruelty, the abuse, the thing that is destroying someone you love, and hate it most fiercely in your own heart, where you can actually fight it. Then love the person, as he does, enough to want him free of it.

Does following a righteous King mean I have to be grim? No. This King is anointed with the oil of gladness, and those who share his kingdom share his joy. Holiness and gladness are not opposites; in him they are one thing. A Christian who is serious about sin but has no joy has understood half the psalm. The sceptre is straight, and the throne is a wedding throne: Psalm 45 is a love song. Obey him gladly, because the one you serve is glad.

In a sentence. About the angels he says, He makes his angels winds, and his servants flames of fire. But to the Son he says, Your throne, O God, lasts for ever and ever; your royal sceptre is a sceptre of justice. You have loved what is right and hated wrongdoing; that is why God, your God, has set you above your companions by anointing you with the oil of joy.

On a Tuesday. Pick one area of your life where you tolerate what Christ hates: a habit of speech, a resentment, a dishonesty at work. Bring it under his sceptre today by naming it to him and taking one concrete step against it. And then do something the anointed King would do with gladness: thank him for a good gift, sing on the way to work, rejoice with someone who is rejoicing. His rule is straight, and it is glad.

For worship. Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever. Every other throne in history has been a chair waiting for its next occupant; this one has never changed hands and never will. The King who sits on it loved righteousness when it cost him the cross, and hated wickedness enough to bear its punishment for others. He was anointed with the oil of gladness, and he wants his people at the wedding. The Bridegroom of Psalm 45 is God, and his bride is a church of forgiven sinners.

verseByVerse.quote: And, “You, Lord, laid the foundation of the earth in the beginning, and the heavens are the work of your hands; they will perish, but you remain; they will all wear out like a garment, like a robe you will roll them up, like a garment they will be changed. But you are the same, and your years will have no end.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
And, “You, Lord, laid the foundation of the earth in the beginning, and the heavens are the work of your hands; they will perish, but you remain; they will all wear out like a garment, like a robe you will roll them up, like a garment they will be changed. But you are the same, and your years will have no end.”

And, You, Lord, laid the foundation of the earth in the beginning. The quotations keep coming, and this one is the boldest of the seven. It is Psalm 102:25–27, and the psalm is a lament: a man in deep affliction, whose days are like an evening shadow, who turns from his own frailty to the permanence of God. The one he addresses in these verses is unmistakably the LORD, Yahweh, the God of Israel, the creator of heaven and earth. And the writer of Hebrews says: this is the Father speaking to the Son.

Texts about God are texts about him. Take the measure of that. A psalm addressed to Yahweh, about the making of the world and the unchangeableness of the divine nature, is quoted as words spoken to Jesus. It is the same move Paul makes in Philippians 2 with Isaiah 45, where every knee bows to the LORD and the knee bows to Jesus. It is the strongest form the New Testament’s teaching about Christ takes: not merely that Jesus is like God, but that texts about God are texts about him. What is said of Yahweh is said of Christ. He is the LORD, the Creator. “In the beginning” echoes Genesis 1:1 and John 1:1.

And the heavens are the work of your hands. The creator language returns from verse 2, now in a quotation, so that Scripture itself says what the writer said in his own voice. The Son made everything. The hands that shaped the heavens were later held out to Thomas, with the marks still in them.

They will perish, but you remain. Here is the contrast the quotation exists for. “Perish” (apolountai): the present creation is not eternal. “Remain” (diameneis): continue, endure throughout. The most permanent-seeming things there are, earth and sky and the ground under your feet, are the temporary items in this comparison. The Son is the one who lasts.

They will all wear out like a garment, like a robe you will roll them up. The universe as an old coat. “Wear out” (palaiōthēsontai) means grow old; creation is like clothing that ages and frays. “Roll them up” (helixeis) means fold up, like a cloak. It is a domestic and slightly startling image: creation handled the way a man handles clothing he has finished with, folded and set aside (Isaiah 34:4; Revelation 6:14). The Son will do with the stars what you do with a jacket at the end of the day.

Like a garment they will be changed. “Changed” (allagēsontai): not annihilated but transformed. The old creation will give way to new heavens and a new earth (2 Peter 3:10–13; Revelation 21:1), and creation itself will be set free from its bondage to decay (Romans 8:19–21). A garment changed is replaced with something better, not with nothing.

But you are the same, and your years will have no end. “The same” (ho autos): unchanging, immutable. It is the flat, unadorned statement of unchangeableness, and in this letter it is not an abstraction. Hebrews is written to people whose world was coming apart: property confiscated, community shunned, some imprisoned (10:32–34). To them the writer says: the things you thought were solid are the garments, and the one you are being tempted to leave is the one who does not change. He will say it again in the plainest form: Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever (13:8). In a world of decay and change, Christ is the one unchanging reality.

What it does not mean. It does not mean creation is worthless because it will pass away. It is God’s good work, and it will be renewed. Nor does the Son’s unchangeableness mean he did not truly become human; he took on human nature without ceasing to be God.

If the world will be rolled up, does it matter how I care for it? Yes. The world is the work of Christ’s hands, and that is reason enough to treat it with respect. Changed is not destroyed: God will renew this creation, not throw it away, and our bodies too will be raised, not discarded. So work done well in this world, kindness to neighbours, care for what God made, is not wasted. What the passage forbids is putting your final trust in anything that can wear out. Enjoy the garment, look after it, and do not mistake it for the one who wears it.

How does an unchanging Christ help me when my life is falling apart? Because he is the one fixed point when everything else moves. Your health may change, your work, your marriage, your church, your own feelings about God. He does not. The love he had for you before you were born is the love he has for you on the worst day of your life. His promises do not expire, his sacrifice does not lose its power, and his intercession does not pause. When nothing feels solid, do not look for a solid circumstance. Look at him, and say to him the words of this psalm: you are the same.

In a sentence. And he also says, In the beginning, Lord, you laid the foundations of the earth, and the heavens are what your hands have made. They will pass away, but you will remain; they will all grow old like clothing. You will roll them up like a cloak, and like clothing they will be replaced. But you stay the same, and your years will never come to an end.

On a Tuesday. Make a short list of the things you most depend on for stability: a job, a person, your health, your savings, your reputation. Beside each one write a single word: garment. Not because they are worthless, but because they will wear. Then write beneath the list what the psalm says of Christ, you remain, and pray through it, handing each thing back to him.

For worship. The psalmist was dying, his days like a lengthening shadow, his bones burning like a furnace, and he lifted his eyes from his own fading to the God who does not fade. Hebrews tells us whose face he was seeing. It was the Son, who laid the foundations of the earth and will fold up the heavens like a cloak, and who in between took our fading flesh, let it wear out on a cross, and rose with it renewed. Everything grows old except him, and he has promised to make all things new.

verseByVerse.quote: And to which of the angels has he ever said, “Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet”? Are they not all ministering spirits sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation?
verseByVerse.commentary:
And to which of the angels has he ever said, “Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet”? Are they not all ministering spirits sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation?

And to which of the angels has he ever said. The seventh and last quotation returns to the form of verse 5, framing the whole series. The chapter opened and closes with the same question, and the answer to both is: to none of them.

Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet. This is Psalm 110:1, the single most quoted Old Testament verse in the New Testament (Matthew 22:44; Acts 2:34–35; 1 Corinthians 15:25; Hebrews 10:12–13). Jesus himself used it to silence the Pharisees, showing that the Messiah is David’s Lord and not merely his son (Mark 12:35–37), and Peter preached it at Pentecost. Hebrews will return to Psalm 110 again and again, since its fourth verse supplies the Melchizedek priesthood that dominates chapters 5 to 7. Two things are given to the Son here that are given to no creature. A place: at my right hand, the position of royal authority. And a promise: that his enemies will be subdued, and that he may sit while it happens. Ancient kings placed their feet on the necks of conquered enemies (Joshua 10:24). Christ reigns now, and his enemies are being subdued, the last enemy being death (1 Corinthians 15:25–26).

Until. This is the word that tells the reader where he is standing in the story. The enemies are not yet a footstool. The subduing is under way and is not finished, which is exactly why the letter’s readers are suffering and why the writer has to argue at all. We live between the sitting and the footstool. The King is already enthroned; the victory is already certain; the last enemy is still in the field.

Are they not all ministering spirits sent out to serve. Then verse 14 closes the chapter by answering the question it raised, and the answer is not what the argument has led us to expect. Having spent nine verses establishing that angels are inferior, the writer might have dismissed them. Instead he says what they are for. “Ministering” (leitourgika) means serving, performing service, and “spirits” (pneumata) recalls the winds of verse 7. All angels, even the highest, are servants. “Sent out” (apostellomena) is present tense: continually being sent. “To serve” (eis diakonian) is for service, ministry.

For the sake of those who are to inherit salvation. Angels are servants, and the ones they are sent to serve are us. That is the sting in the tail of the whole chapter. The glorious beings through whom the law was given are in the service of ordinary struggling Christians in a house church somewhere, dispatched for the benefit of people the world would not look at twice. Scripture shows them protecting, guiding and ministering many times (Psalm 34:7; 91:11; Acts 12:7–10; Matthew 18:10). The beings the readers were tempted to honour above Christ actually serve Christ’s people. And the word “inherit” (klēronomein) ties back to verse 2 and closes the circle. The Son is heir of all things; those who are his inherit salvation. What is his by right becomes theirs by gift, and the angels, who inherit nothing, are sent out to look after the heirs.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we should pray to angels or seek contact with them (Colossians 2:18). They serve at God’s command, not ours. Nor does it give a basis for the idea of each person having a personal guardian angel assigned for life, though angels certainly do watch over God’s people.

What about Matthew 18:10 and Peter’s angel? Jesus says of his little ones that in heaven their angels always see the face of his Father (Matthew 18:10), and the disciples in Acts thought it was Peter’s angel at the door (Acts 12:15). These texts show that God’s angels are concerned with his people, and that the least of them are not overlooked in heaven. They do not teach that each person has one angel assigned to him for life; the second is only what frightened disciples supposed. This verse speaks of angels as a company sent to serve all who will inherit salvation. We can be sure that God sends his angels for his people; we are not told more, and should not invent it.

Why do I never see angels, if they are serving me? Because their service is usually hidden, and that is by design. Most of what God does for his people is done out of sight: dangers turned aside that you never knew were coming, strength given in an hour you thought you could not survive. Elisha’s servant saw only the enemy army until God opened his eyes to the hills full of horses and chariots of fire (2 Kings 6:15–17). You do not need to see them, and you should not try to contact them. Trust the God who sends them, and thank him for protection you will only fully know in glory.

In a sentence. And to which of the angels did God ever say, Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a stool for your feet? Are not all the angels spirits who serve, sent out to help those who will inherit salvation?

On a Tuesday. When you feel small, overlooked or alone in your faithfulness, remember who has been sent for you. Then take the hint the angels give: serve. Find one person this week who will inherit salvation, a weary believer, an elderly saint, a young Christian, and do for them something unseen and unthanked. You will be doing the work of angels, and serving the King who sits at the right hand.

For worship. The King sits, and the battle goes on, and the outcome is not in doubt. Every enemy of his people, sin and Satan and death itself, is on its way to becoming a footstool. And while he waits, the Son sends the armies of heaven not to guard his throne, which needs no guard, but to look after his heirs. The mightiest creatures God ever made are on errands for people who trust his Son. Such is the honour the Son has given those he purchased: what is his by right, he has made theirs by gift.
verseByVerse.note: Psalm 110 is the Old Testament passage most often quoted in the New.
