4.title: A Rest That Remains: The Throne of Grace
4.overview:
Chapter 4 develops one of the most original arguments in the New Testament. The rest God promised was not fully given under Joshua; otherwise, why would God say through David, centuries later, “Today, if you hear his voice”? So the rest remains. And it is not a land or a day, but a share in God’s own Sabbath rest: the rest of finished work. To enter it is to stop working to justify ourselves and trust what Christ has finished.

The chapter ends with a sword and an invitation. God’s word lays us bare; nothing is hidden. And then: since we have a great high priest who sympathises with our weakness, let us draw near with confidence to the throne of grace.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — There Remains a Sabbath Rest
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The promise of entering God’s rest still stands, so let us take care that none of us falls short. The wilderness generation heard good news, but it did not benefit them because they did not receive it with faith. We who believe enter that rest. God’s rest has existed since he rested on the seventh day, and centuries after Joshua God still said “Today”. So a Sabbath rest remains for God’s people: to rest from our works as God did from his. Let us strive to enter it.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Rest That Remains

Psalm 95 still says today centuries after Joshua, so the land was never the rest itself. What remains is a Sabbath rest: ceasing from our own works as God did from his.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The wilderness generation heard good news, and it did not benefit them because it was not united with faith.

Now: Strive to enter that rest. Trusting God is harder work than being busy for him.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, while the promise of entering his rest still stands, let us fear lest any of you should seem to have failed to reach it. For good news came to us just as to them, but the message they heard did not benefit them, because they were not united by faith with those who listened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, while the promise of entering his rest still stands, let us fear lest any of you should seem to have failed to reach it. For good news came to us just as to them, but the message they heard did not benefit them, because they were not united by faith with those who listened.

Meaning first. Hebrews 4 continues the warning of chapter 3 and explains what God’s rest really is. The promise of entering God’s rest still stands, so the readers must take care not to fall short of it; the wilderness generation heard good news too, but it did not help them because they did not believe (vv. 1–2). Those who believe do enter that rest (v. 3). What rest is it? Not merely Canaan: God’s own rest began on the seventh day of creation, when he finished his works (vv. 3–5). Since Psalm 95, written long after Joshua led Israel into Canaan, still speaks of entering God’s rest today, Joshua cannot have given the final rest (vv. 6–8). So there remains a Sabbath rest for God’s people: resting from our own works as God rested from his (vv. 9–10). Therefore we must strive to enter it (v. 11). And we cannot hide behind religious appearances, because God’s word is living and active, sharper than any sword, exposing the heart, and everything lies naked before the God to whom we must give account (vv. 12–13). But we are not left alone with that exposure: we have a great high priest, Jesus the Son of God, who has passed through the heavens, who sympathises with our weakness, having been tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin. So let us hold fast and draw near with confidence to the throne of grace, to receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need (vv. 14–16).

Therefore, while the promise of entering his rest still stands. That is the foundation of the whole chapter, and it is a mercy. “Promise” (epangelia). “Still stands” (kataleipomenēs): being left behind, remaining open. The last generation forfeited it; the promise did not lapse with them. The offer of God’s rest was not withdrawn when Israel failed; it is still open now. God’s offer outlived the people who refused it, and it has outlived every generation since.

Let us fear. A striking instruction, and the New Testament does not often give it in this form. “Fear” (phobēthōmen) is not the fear of a God who might turn on us without warning; the same chapter ends by sending its readers boldly to a throne of grace. It is the fear appropriate to standing near something enormous and being capable of walking past it: a healthy, reverent fear of falling short, the seriousness of someone who knows what is at stake (Philippians 2:12; 1 Peter 1:17). And again it is let us, not you must. The preacher stands inside his own warning.

Lest any of you should seem to have failed to reach it. The phrasing is unexpectedly gentle. He does not say lest any of you fail; he says lest any should seem (dokē: appear, be found, be judged) to have failed. The writer will not pronounce on who is in and who is out. He is warning against even the appearance of falling short, which leaves the judgement where it belongs and still leaves the warning its full weight. “Failed to reach” (hysterēkenai) means to fall short, to come too late, to lag behind, like a traveller who arrives after the city gates have closed for the night, or a runner who drops away from the pack and is not seen again.

For good news came to us just as to them. That sentence should stop a reader, because it says the wilderness generation had good news preached to them (euēngelismenoi, we have had the gospel preached). Not the same details, but the same thing in substance: a promise from God about a rest they had not seen, to be received by trusting him. They heard the promise of the land. We have heard the greater good news of Christ. The God of the exodus and the God of the cross deal with people the same way: he promises, and calls them to believe.

But the message they heard did not benefit them. “Did not benefit” (ouk ōphelēsen): did not profit. Hearing is not enough. The wilderness generation had the best preacher in their history, Moses, and the clearest content, and it did them no good.

Because they were not united by faith with those who listened. The word for united (synkekerasmenous) means mixed together, compounded, blended, the image of two things combined into one. Some manuscripts read it as the message not being combined with faith in the hearers; others as the hearers not being united in faith with those who truly listened, Joshua and Caleb. Either way, the message went in and did not combine with anything. It was heard and not absorbed. The word must be received with faith to benefit. Food that is not eaten does not nourish, however good the meal.

Why the same sermon does different things. Press this, because it answers a question people ask about their own churchgoing. What makes preaching profitable is not the eloquence of the preacher or the accuracy of the content, both of which the wilderness generation had in Moses. It is whether faith mixes with what is heard. The same sermon in the same room profits one person and does nothing whatever to the man beside him, and Hebrews says the difference is not in the sermon.

What it does not mean. It does not mean faith is a work that adds to the gospel. Faith is the empty hand that receives it. Nor does “let us fear” contradict assurance; it is the fear that drives us to Christ, not away from him.

How do I mix the word with faith when I hear it? By taking it as God speaking to you, and answering him. Before the sermon or the reading, ask the Spirit to open your heart. While you listen, listen for a promise to trust, a command to obey, a warning to heed, or a glimpse of Christ to adore. Afterwards, do not just evaluate how good it was; say to God, I believe this, and tell him what you will do about it. Talk about it with someone over lunch. Faith is not a feeling that comes over you during a good sermon; it is the act of leaning your weight on what God has said.

In a sentence. So, since God’s promise of entering his rest is still open, let us be careful that none of you turns out to have fallen short of it. We have had the good news announced to us just as they did, but the message they heard did them no good, because they did not combine it with faith.

On a Tuesday. Are you hearing God’s word without mixing it with faith? As you read Scripture today, stop at one verse and respond to it out loud: believe it, trust it, act on it. And after next Sunday’s sermon, write one sentence before you leave the building: what God said, and what you are going to do because he said it.

For worship. The promise still stands. Generations have refused it, and God has not withdrawn it. He went on offering rest to Israel through Moses, through Joshua, through David, through the prophets, and at last he offered it in his Son, with nail-scarred hands outstretched: come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Matthew 11:28). The God who keeps a door open that long, for people that faithless, is a God of astonishing patience. The rest is his, and he still wants to share it.

verseByVerse.quote: For we who have believed enter that rest, as he has said, “As I swore in my wrath, ’They shall not enter my rest,’” although his works were finished from the foundation of the world. For he has somewhere spoken of the seventh day in this way: “And God rested on the seventh day from all his works.” And again in this passage he said, “They shall not enter my rest.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we who have believed enter that rest, as he has said, “As I swore in my wrath, ‘They shall not enter my rest,’” although his works were finished from the foundation of the world. For he has somewhere spoken of the seventh day in this way: “And God rested on the seventh day from all his works.” And again in this passage he said, “They shall not enter my rest.”

For we who have believed enter that rest. Present tense, and it is the answer to verse 2. Where they did not mix the word with faith, these have, and the entering is happening now. “Have believed” (pisteusantes) is aorist: those who came to faith. “Enter” (eiserchometha) is present: are entering. Believers enter God’s rest now, in part: rest from the burden of earning salvation, peace with God, rest of conscience (Matthew 11:28–29; Romans 5:1). And they will enter it fully in glory. The rest is both present and future, begun and not yet finished.

As he has said, As I swore in my wrath, They shall not enter my rest. Then the writer does something intricate, and it repays following slowly, because the argument of the whole chapter turns on it. He quotes the oath of Psalm 95:11 again. The negative proves the positive: unbelievers are excluded, so believers enter. God did not swear that nobody would enter; he swore that those would not.

Although his works were finished from the foundation of the world. Then a clause that seems to come from nowhere, and the point is about timing. “Finished” (genēthentōn): completed. God speaks in the psalm of my rest as something people might enter or fail to enter, but his own rest has existed since the seventh day. So the rest in question cannot be something God started providing at Sinai or in Canaan. It has been there since creation was finished. It is God’s own rest, and he invites his people to share it.

For he has somewhere spoken of the seventh day in this way: And God rested on the seventh day from all his works. That is Genesis 2:2, and it supplies the definition. God rested (katepausen, ceased) not because he was tired, for he does not faint or grow weary (Isaiah 40:28), but because his work of creation was complete. God’s rest is not a nap after exertion. It is the settled satisfaction of a maker who has finished and found it very good.

The day with no evening. And notice what is missing from the Genesis account, which ancient readers noticed too. Every other day of creation ends with the refrain, and there was evening and there was morning. The seventh day has no evening. It is left open, and the writer is arguing that it is still open now. God’s rest has no end. It is an ongoing state of completed satisfaction, and it has been waiting for guests since the world began.

And again in this passage he said, They shall not enter my rest. Verse 5 sets the two texts side by side once more. Putting Genesis 2:2 and Psalm 95:11 together, the rest Israel failed to enter was God’s own Sabbath rest, of which Canaan was only a picture. Two facts are held together. There is a rest, and it dates from the world’s foundation. And there are people who did not get in. The conclusion is not yet stated, but it is now inevitable: if the rest has existed since creation, and a whole generation missed it, then the rest is still there and someone else may enter. That is what verse 6 will say, and it is a remarkable way to read Scripture, drawing a doctrine of present opportunity out of the silence at the end of a day in Genesis.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God stopped all activity on the seventh day; he continues to uphold all things (1:3; John 5:17). He ceased from the work of creating.

What is this rest like now, if I have believed? It is the rest of a forgiven person who no longer has to prove himself to God. Your standing is settled, so you do not need to earn his favour each morning or fear losing it each evening. It is rest of conscience: guilt answered by the blood of Christ. It is rest from the restless search for meaning, because you have found the one you were made for. It does not mean an easy life; these readers were suffering. But underneath the trouble there is a floor that does not move. Augustine put it in a prayer: you have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.

In a sentence. Now we who have believed are entering that rest, just as God said, So I declared on oath in my anger, They shall never enter my rest. And yet his works have been finished since the creation of the world. For somewhere he has spoken about the seventh day in these words: On the seventh day God rested from all his works. And again, in the passage above, he says, They shall never enter my rest.

On a Tuesday. Notice today where you are still working for God’s approval: the anxious overwork in ministry, the guilt after a poor quiet time, the feeling that he must be disappointed in you. Stop at that moment and say: I have believed, and I am entering his rest. Then do the thing in front of you as a child at home, not as a servant on probation.

For worship. On the seventh day God looked at everything he had made and found it very good, and he rested in the joy of it. He has never closed that day. It has no evening, and he has been inviting creatures into it ever since. Sin shut us out, and his Son opened the way again by finishing a greater work and saying, it is finished. Now the God who rested from creation invites the people he has redeemed to rest with him, in a joy that will never end.

verseByVerse.quote: Since therefore it remains for some to enter it, and those who formerly received the good news failed to enter because of disobedience, again he appoints a certain day, “Today,” saying through David so long afterward, in the words already quoted, “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.” For if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken of another day later on.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since therefore it remains for some to enter it, and those who formerly received the good news failed to enter because of disobedience, again he appoints a certain day, “Today,” saying through David so long afterward, in the words already quoted, “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.” For if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken of another day later on.

Since therefore it remains for some to enter it. The conclusion lands. “Remains” (apoleipetai): is left over, still open. The rest was not abolished when the wilderness generation forfeited it; a vacancy was created. God’s purpose is that some will enter his rest. The failure of one generation did not cancel his plan.

And those who formerly received the good news failed to enter because of disobedience. The wilderness generation again. The word is the one from 3:18: unpersuadable. In this letter unbelief and disobedience are the same failure seen from two sides. Not believing God is not obeying him, because his word came as a promise to be trusted.

Again he appoints a certain day, Today. “Appoints” (horizei): sets, defines, marks out. God fixed a new day of opportunity. And now the writer plays his decisive card, which is a point about dates.

Saying through David so long afterward. That is the whole argument in a phrase. Psalm 95 is attributed to David in the Greek translation. David lived about four hundred years after Moses and Joshua. And in it God is still saying today, still warning people not to harden their hearts, still holding a rest open. If the promise of rest had been fully realised in Canaan, why would David still be offering it, centuries later?

For if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken of another day later on. Verse 8 draws the inference and names the man. Joshua did give them rest, in the ordinary sense. The book bearing his name says the LORD gave them rest on every side, and that not one word of all the good promises had failed (Joshua 21:44–45; 23:1). They crossed the Jordan, took the land and settled it. And the writer says: evidently that was not it. Because centuries later God was still offering a rest to people who were already living in the land. A man farming his own field in Judah under David was, on any ordinary reading, in the rest, and God tells him not to harden his heart today, lest he fail to enter.

Joshua and Jesus. In Greek, Joshua and Jesus are the same name (Iēsous), meaning the LORD saves. The first readers heard it at once. The first Joshua brought Israel into an earthly land, and they still needed a rest. The greater Joshua, Jesus, brings his people into God’s eternal rest. The land was never the thing itself. It was a picture, and possessing it did not settle the question. That is precisely what the readers of this letter needed to hear, since what they were being drawn back to was the whole apparatus of land, temple and ancestral religion: the very things that had never given anybody final rest.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Joshua failed or that Canaan was not a real gift. It was real, but it was a shadow of something greater, as the whole Old Testament is.

Is the promised rest the same as heaven? It includes heaven, but it is larger than a place you go when you die. It begins now, when you trust Christ and cease from trying to save yourself (v. 3). It continues through this life as peace with God in the middle of trouble. It comes to its fullness when Christ returns and his people enter the new creation, the true promised land, where there is no more death or mourning or pain (Revelation 21:4). Canaan pictured it; heaven anticipates it; the new heavens and new earth complete it. The rest is finally not a location but a sharing in God’s own joy, wherever he is.

In a sentence. So it is still true that some are to enter that rest, and since those who first had the good news preached to them did not enter because they disobeyed, God again set a particular day, calling it Today. He spoke of it through David a long time later, in the words already quoted: Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts. For if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken later about another day.

On a Tuesday. Ask what you are expecting to give you rest: the next holiday, retirement, a paid-off mortgage, a settled family, a better church. None of these is wrong; each is a Canaan, real and good and not the thing itself. Enjoy them as gifts, and stop asking them to be your rest. Tell Jesus, the greater Joshua, that you are looking to him for what no land can give.

For worship. The first Joshua led a nation across a river into fields and vineyards, and they still needed rest. The second Joshua, Jesus, crossed the river of death itself and came up on the far bank alive, and the land he leads his people into is God’s own rest. He did not merely point the way; he went first, conquered the enemy, and holds the door open. Every Canaan in this world fades. The rest he gives never does.

verseByVerse.quote: So then, there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God, for whoever has entered God’s rest has also rested from his works as God did from his.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So then, there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God, for whoever has entered God’s rest has also rested from his works as God did from his.

So then, there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God. The word here is different from the one used everywhere else in the chapter. Throughout, the writer has said katapausis, rest. Here, once, he coins or reaches for sabbatismos, a Sabbath-keeping, a Sabbath celebration. It occurs nowhere else in the Greek Bible. The change of word is the point. He has been arguing from Genesis 2 that God’s own rest is what is on offer, and now he names it accordingly. What remains is not merely relief but a festive Sabbath rest, sharing in God’s own celebration of his finished work. “Remains” (apoleipetai) keeps the tense of the whole argument. Not is promised, not will one day be created. It is there now, still waiting, still to come in its fullness. And “the people of God” are all who believe.

For whoever has entered God’s rest has also rested from his works as God did from his. Here is the definition, and it is the most practically searching sentence in the chapter. To enter this rest is to stop working, in the way God stopped. And God did not stop because he was tired or because he had run out of time. He stopped because the work was finished, and there was nothing left to add to it. Applied to a person, that is the end of religious self-effort. Entering God’s rest means ceasing from our own works: ceasing from trying to earn salvation by our efforts, and resting in Christ’s finished work. To the one who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness (Romans 4:5). The man who has entered has laid down the attempt to establish himself before God, because someone else has said it is finished and sat down (1:3). He is not resting from labour; he is resting from works, from the whole enterprise of making himself acceptable. It may also refer to the final rest after the labours of this life: blessed are the dead who die in the Lord, that they may rest from their labours (Revelation 14:13). Both are true. Now we rest from works as a way of salvation; then we will rest from all toil and suffering.

Why going back was a refusal to rest. That is why the readers’ temptation was so serious and so understandable. Going back to the sacrifices meant going back to a system where the work was never finished and no priest ever sat down. It would have felt like devotion. It was, in the terms of this chapter, a refusal to rest. And the rest is not merely a future condition. The verb in verse 3 is present: we who have believed enter. There is a Sabbath still to come, and there is a resting available this afternoon, to anyone willing to stop.

Where Christians differ: is the weekly Sabbath still binding on Christians? Seventh-day Adventists and Seventh Day Baptists hold that the seventh-day Sabbath is still binding. Many in the Reformed and Puritan tradition, following the Westminster Confession, hold that the Sabbath commandment continues as a creation ordinance (Genesis 2:3), transferred to Sunday as the Christian Sabbath, with strict rest required. Others see the Sabbath as wholly fulfilled in Christ, with no special day required. Verdict: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, who gives the true rest it pointed to (Matthew 11:28–12:8; Colossians 2:16–17). Christians are not bound to the Old Testament Sabbath regulations. Yet the pattern of one day in seven is a creation gift, and the early church gathered on the first day of the week, the Lord’s Day, to celebrate Christ’s resurrection (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2; Revelation 1:10). Keeping the Lord’s Day for worship, rest and fellowship is a great privilege and wise practice, not a legal burden or a means of earning favour. Those who keep a stricter Sabbath should be respected (Romans 14:5–6).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should be idle or stop doing good works. Resting from works as a means of salvation frees us for good works as fruit of salvation (Ephesians 2:8–10). Nor does it mean the final rest has fully arrived; it remains.

How do I rest from my works when I am naturally a striver? Begin by noticing what you are trying to prove, and to whom. Strivers often carry a quiet belief that God’s love is in proportion to their output. Answer it with the gospel every day: Christ has finished the work, and you are accepted in him, not on your performance. Then let that truth shape your week. Keep the Lord’s Day as a gift: worship, rest, enjoy people, leave the unfinished work unfinished, and discover that the world, and God, carry on without you. Good works will still flow, but from rest rather than toward it, which makes them gladder and lighter.

In a sentence. So a Sabbath rest is still waiting for God’s people; for anyone who enters God’s rest also rests from their own work, just as God did from his.

On a Tuesday. Plan next Sunday now. Decide what you will lay down for the day: emails, the shopping, the to-do list. Decide how you will fill it: gathering with God’s people, a meal, a walk, an afternoon with family, a long prayer. Treat it as a weekly rehearsal of the rest that remains: not a rule to keep God pleased, but a gift to remind you that he already is.

For worship. God finished his work and rested, and he invited his people to rest with him. They could not, because they would not stop working for themselves. Then the Son came and did the work they could not do, every bit of it, down to the last drop of blood, and cried that it was finished, and lay in a tomb through the Sabbath, and rose on the first day of a new week. Since then his people have gathered on that day to celebrate a rest they did not earn. A Sabbath-feast remains, and it is the joy of God himself, shared with the children his Son has brought home.

verseByVerse.quote: Let us therefore strive to enter that rest, so that no one may fall by the same sort of disobedience.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let us therefore strive to enter that rest, so that no one may fall by the same sort of disobedience.

Let us therefore strive to enter that rest. It is one of the great paradoxes of Scripture, and the writer does not soften it. Work hard at resting. Make every effort to stop making an effort. The verb (spoudasōmen) means to be diligent, to exert oneself, to hurry, and its object is the rest. The paradox is real, but it is not a contradiction, and the previous verse has already resolved it. We do not strive to earn salvation. The works being rested from are works of self-establishment, the attempt to make oneself acceptable. The striving being commanded is the effort of trusting: to keep believing, to resist hardening, to hold fast (3:6, 14; 2 Peter 1:10), continuing to take God at his word when everything in the circumstances argues against it.

Harder than being busy. And anyone who has tried it knows it is effort. It is far easier to be busy for God than to believe him. Religious activity is within our reach; resting on a promise, when the property has been confiscated and the neighbours have turned, is not a passive condition at all. It has to be fought for. The effort is the effort of faith, which keeps trusting and obeying.

So that no one may fall by the same sort of disobedience. The wilderness generation is held up one last time. “Fall” (pesē) echoes the bodies that fell in the wilderness (3:17). “Same sort” (tō autō hypodeigmati) is literally the same example: the same pattern, the same shape of failure (1 Corinthians 10:6, 11). And note the concern once more: no one. Singular, individual, the same anxiety as 3:12 and 4:1. The writer keeps scanning the congregation for the one person quietly slipping, and he asks the whole body to do the same.

A failure of nerve. There is a final irony in the verse worth carrying away. The wilderness generation fell because they would not go in. They stood at the border of a good land, heard the spies’ report of giants and walled cities, and judged it too dangerous. Their disobedience was not a wild plunge into sin but a failure of nerve at the edge of a promise. That is the pattern the readers are told to avoid, and it is the one most Christians are actually in danger of.

What it does not mean. It does not mean salvation is by works. The rest we strive to enter is the rest from works. The striving is to keep trusting Christ and not drift back to self-reliance or unbelief.

If God keeps me, why must I strive? Because God keeps you by making you strive. Perseverance is God’s work in you and your work at the same time: work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure (Philippians 2:12–13). Your effort does not compete with his grace; it is the form his grace takes in you. A ship crossing the sea is carried by the wind, and the sailors still trim the sails all night. If you find a desire in yourself to keep going with Christ, that desire is his gift, and the warning is his way of strengthening it.

In a sentence. So let us make every effort to enter that rest, so that none of us falls by following their example of disobedience.

On a Tuesday. What could cause you to drift from trusting Christ: busyness, a grievance, a secret sin, fear of what obedience will cost? Name the giant at your border. Then strive against it today with the ordinary weapons: prayer, Scripture, confession, staying close to God’s people. And ask yourself where God is calling you to step forward in trust rather than hold back in fear.

For worship. The Son of God strove for our rest. He set his face to go to Jerusalem, sweated in the garden, and fought through the darkness of the cross, so that the rest would be open to us. Now he strengthens the weak hands of those who follow, and prays for them that their faith may not fail (Luke 22:32). We strive because he strove first, and we will enter because he has already gone in, and holds the door.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–16 — Laid Bare, and Invited In
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The writer warns that God’s word is alive and at work, cutting more sharply than any blade, reaching to the deepest parts of a person and exposing the real thoughts and motives of the heart. No creature can hide from God; everything lies open before the one to whom we must give account. But there is an invitation alongside the warning. We have a great high priest who has passed into heaven, Jesus, God’s Son, so we should keep holding to our confession. He is able to feel for our weaknesses, because he was tested in every way as we are, yet without sin. So we can come confidently to God’s throne of grace, to receive mercy and find grace to help us when we need it.
verseByVerse.theology:
Why the Exposure Comes First

The word lays us bare, and only then does the writer say, “since then we have a great high priest”. The one who sees through us is the one who sympathises with us.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Drawing near was once the privilege of priests alone.

Now: Come to the throne of grace with confidence — mercy for what lies behind, grace for what lies ahead, help that arrives when it is needed.

verseByVerse.quote: For the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing to the division of soul and of spirit, of joints and of marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing to the division of soul and of spirit, of joints and of marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart.

For the word of God. The for ties this to what came before, and the connection is easily missed. It explains why we must strive (v. 11): God’s word sees through every pretence. This is not a general statement about the Bible dropped into the argument. The writer has just spent eleven verses proving that a psalm written by David still says today to people a thousand years later. Now he says why. “The word of God” (ho logos tou theou) is God’s spoken and written word, here especially the warnings of Psalm 95 just quoted, and all Scripture.

Is living and active. “Living” (zōn): alive, because it comes from the living God (3:12). It does not become a historical document. It keeps speaking. “Active” (energēs, from which we get energetic) means effective, powerful, at work. Scripture is not a dead letter. It does things: it convicts, converts, comforts and sanctifies. It goes out from God’s mouth and does not return empty (Isaiah 55:10–11); it is like a fire and like a hammer that breaks the rock in pieces (Jeremiah 23:29); it is at work in those who believe (1 Thessalonians 2:13). Hebrews has been demonstrating that all chapter, since a sentence in Genesis about the seventh day turned out to be doing something more than a thousand years after it was written.

Sharper than any two-edged sword. The word for sword here (machaira) is not the great battle blade but the short one, the Roman short sword used for close combat, the surgeon’s and the assassin’s instrument (Ephesians 6:17; Revelation 1:16). “Two-edged” (distomos) is literally two-mouthed, which is a fine touch in a passage about a word that speaks.

Piercing to the division of soul and of spirit, of joints and of marrow. “Piercing” (diiknoumenos) is penetrating right through. The writer is not offering a psychology here, and it is a mistake to build one from him. He is piling up pairs of things that cannot ordinarily be got between: soul (psychē) and spirit (pneuma), joints (harmoi) and marrow (myeloi). Where does soul end and spirit begin? Where exactly does a joint stop and the marrow start? Nobody can find the seam. This word can. The point is not anatomical precision but total penetration: nothing is beyond its reach.

And discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart. The adjective is kritikos, able to judge, to sift, to pass verdict; our word critical. And the two objects are exact. Thoughts (enthymēseis): what passes through the mind, reflections, ideas. Intentions (ennoiai): the purposes underneath, the motives, what we are actually after. That second one is the sting. Most of us can give an honest account of our thoughts. Almost nobody can give an honest account of his motives, because the mind is expert at supplying respectable reasons for what it wanted anyway. The word of God is here described as the instrument that gets between the stated reason and the real one. We do not judge Scripture; it judges us.

What the readers needed. That is exactly what this congregation needed. They were, presumably, telling themselves that returning to the old ways was a matter of conscience, or family, or prudence. The writer says there is a word that can divide the reason from the motive, and it is currently being read aloud to them.

Where Christians differ: are soul and spirit two different parts of a person? Some teach a threefold view of human nature (body, soul and spirit as three distinct parts), using this verse and 1 Thessalonians 5:23. Verdict: Scripture generally uses soul and spirit interchangeably for the immaterial part of a person (Luke 1:46–47; John 12:27 and 13:21; Matthew 10:28). The body-and-soul view (dichotomy) fits the overall biblical teaching best. This verse does not teach that soul and spirit are separate components; like joints and marrow, it pictures the word cutting to the very core of a person.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Scripture works like magic apart from the Spirit. The Spirit uses the word. Nor does it mean the “word of God” here refers primarily to Jesus as the Word (John 1:1), though he is the one who speaks it.

Why does the Bible sometimes feel dead to me, if it is living? Because the problem is usually on the receiving end, not the sending end. A living word can meet a dull heart, a hurried reading or a mind full of noise. Sometimes it is a season of dryness God uses to deepen trust that does not depend on feelings. Keep reading anyway, slowly, and pray before you start: open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law (Psalm 119:18). Read aloud; read a whole book through; read with others; memorise a verse and turn it over through the day. The word is still at work even when you do not feel it, as seed in the ground is alive before anything shows.

In a sentence. For God’s word is alive and powerful, sharper than any double-edged sword. It cuts right through, to where soul and spirit, joints and marrow meet, and it judges the thoughts and motives of the heart.

On a Tuesday. Read Scripture today and let it read you. Take one passage, and after reading it ask: what thoughts and motives is God exposing in my heart? Write down one motive you would rather not admit, the real reason behind something you did this week. Then bring it to him in the light of the next three verses.

For worship. God has not left us with a book of dead letters. His word is alive because he is alive, and it still does what it did when it said let there be light. It cuts, not to wound for the sake of wounding, but as a surgeon cuts, to heal. It finds the motive we hid even from ourselves, and it does so in order to bring us to the high priest who can deal with it. The sword that lays us open is held by the hand of a Saviour.

verseByVerse.quote: And no creature is hidden from his sight, but all are naked and exposed to the eyes of him to whom we must give account.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And no creature is hidden from his sight, but all are naked and exposed to the eyes of him to whom we must give account.

And no creature is hidden from his sight. The subject shifts without warning from the word to the one who speaks it, and the shift is the point. To be read by the word is to be seen by God. “Creature” (ktisis) is any created thing; “hidden” (aphanēs) is invisible, concealed. Nothing in all creation escapes his knowledge (Psalm 139:1–16; Proverbs 15:3; Jeremiah 23:24).

But all are naked and exposed to the eyes of him. Two words, and both are vivid. “Naked” (gymna) is bare, uncovered, and it carries the whole biblical weight of the word. The first thing sin produced was the impulse to cover up and hide among the trees of the garden. Every religious system since has been in some measure an elaborate rearrangement of fig leaves. The second word, tetrachēlismena, is rarer and harder. It comes from the word for neck, and its uses point several ways. It was used of a wrestler’s hold that seizes the throat and forces the opponent’s face upward so that he cannot look away, of a sacrificial animal whose neck was drawn back to expose the throat for the knife, and of a criminal forced to lift his face to the judge. Every picture says the same thing: the head is held so that the face is turned up and nothing can be concealed. There is no averting the eyes.

To whom we must give account. The phrase is literally with whom is our word (pros hon hēmin ho logos), and it plays on word in verse 12. The word for account is the word for a ledger or a reckoning, and it is the same root (logos) as the word of God in the verse before. God’s word judges us, and we must give our word, our account, to him. The Word we must answer to and the Word that examines us are not two different things. Every person will stand before God (Romans 14:12; 2 Corinthians 5:10).

Stripped in order to be clothed. And here is where the chapter would be unbearable if it stopped. A word that divides motive from motive, a God from whom nothing is hidden, and an account to be rendered. Any honest person reading verses 12 and 13 should feel exposed, and is meant to. That is exactly why the next verse begins with since then. The writer has stripped his readers deliberately, and he has done it in order to tell them who is standing at the throne.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God watches only to condemn. For those in Christ, being fully known is the beginning of being fully loved and healed. The next verses turn immediately to the high priest who sympathises.

Does God see the things I have done in secret, even the shameful ones? Yes, every one of them, and he saw them before you did them. That is terrifying if you are hiding from him, and it is the deepest relief if you belong to Christ. You are not going to be found out; you have been fully known all along, and he loved you and sent his Son anyway (Romans 5:8). So stop spending your strength on concealment. Bring the secret to him by name in confession; he already knows it, and you do not need to soften it. Where it is wise, tell a mature believer too (James 5:16). What is brought into the light with God is covered by the blood of Christ (1 John 1:7–9).

In a sentence. Nothing in all creation is hidden from God. Everything is uncovered and laid bare before the eyes of the one to whom we must give our account.

On a Tuesday. Is there something you have been hiding, from others, from yourself, from God? Write it down in one honest line. Then pray it to God plainly, without excuses, and thank him that he already saw it and that Christ already bore it. If it involves wrong done to someone, take one step today to put it right.

For worship. There is one pair of eyes from which nothing is hidden, and they are the eyes that wept over Jerusalem. The God before whom every throat is bared is the God who bared his own Son’s back to the whip and his own Son’s side to the spear. He sees everything, and he gave everything. To be naked before him is the end of every pretence, and for those in Christ it is the beginning of being clothed in a righteousness that will never be stripped away.

verseByVerse.quote: Since then we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus, the Son of God, let us hold fast our confession. For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since then we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus, the Son of God, let us hold fast our confession. For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin.

Since then we have a great high priest. The pivot of the letter arrives, and the timing is everything. It comes immediately after the most exposing sentence in Hebrews. Naked, laid bare, accountable, and we have a priest. “Great high priest” (archierea megan): Aaron was the high priest; Jesus is the great high priest. The main theme of chapters 4 to 10 begins here.

Who has passed through the heavens. “Passed through” (dielēlythota) is perfect tense: he has gone through, and the result stands. The picture is the Day of Atonement, when the high priest passed through the courts and the curtain into the Most Holy Place, once a year, with blood (Leviticus 16). Jesus has passed through the heavens themselves into the very presence of God (9:24), at his ascension. The tabernacle was a copy; Christ entered the reality.

Jesus, the Son of God. Both names are needed. “Jesus”: his human name, the man from Nazareth who was hungry and tired and wept, the man who suffered. “Son of God”: his divine identity, the one whom angels worship. Both together qualify him to be our high priest: truly human to represent us, truly divine to make his sacrifice infinitely effective. The two titles side by side are the argument of the next verse.

Let us hold fast our confession. “Hold fast” (kratōmen) is grip firmly, take hold strongly. “Confession” (homologia) is the confession named at 3:1, the thing they said publicly and are under pressure to unsay. Notice the order: not hold fast, and then you will have a priest; but we have a great high priest, so hold fast. The grip is a response to the priest, not a way of acquiring one.

For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses. Verse 15 is stated as a double negative because the writer knows what his readers are afraid of. A priest who has passed through the heavens sounds magnificent and remote; the very grandeur of verse 14 might make a struggling person feel he could not possibly understand. So the writer denies it before it can be said out loud. The double negative (not unable) emphasises it: he can and does sympathise. “Sympathise” (sympathēsai) is to suffer with, to feel together with; our word sympathy. Not pity from above, which is what a superior offers an inferior, but feeling with. “Weaknesses” (astheneiai) are frailties, infirmities, limitations: not only sins, but the whole fragility of being human. He is not a distant, unfeeling figure.

But one who in every respect has been tempted as we are. “In every respect” (kata panta): in all things. “Tempted” (pepeirasmenon) is perfect tense: tested, tried, and he still knows it from experience. Jesus faced every kind of temptation humans face: to doubt God, to take shortcuts, to avoid suffering, to seek glory, to give up. Not every specific temptation in every circumstance, but every type, at full force.

Yet without sin. “Without sin” (chōris hamartias): there is the exception promised at 2:17. He never sinned, in thought, word or deed (7:26; 2 Corinthians 5:21; 1 Peter 2:22; 1 John 3:5). And it is important, because it is often misheard as a limitation on his sympathy, as though never having sinned meant he could not understand those who do. The opposite is true, and it is one of the most useful things in this letter. The man who yields to a temptation never discovers how strong it was, because he stopped the pressure early. Only the one who holds out to the end feels its full weight, as a person who never gives in feels the full pressure of the wind. He is not less qualified to sympathise for never having fallen. He is the only person who has ever felt the whole force of what we surrender to.

Where Christians differ: could Jesus have sinned? Some argue that if he could not have sinned, his temptations were not real. Verdict: the Son of God could not sin, because he is God, and God cannot sin (James 1:13). Yet his temptations were real, because his human nature genuinely felt their pull, and he resisted by faith, prayer and the Spirit’s power as a true man. A bridge that cannot collapse is still truly tested by the weight of the trucks that cross it. His impeccability does not lessen his sympathy; it makes his help sure.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jesus’ temptations were identical to ours in every detail, or that he experienced the temptations that arise from already having sinned. It means he knows temptation from the inside, and can help.

Did Jesus face temptations like mine, sexual temptation, despair, addiction? He faced every kind of temptation common to human beings, though not every circumstance: he was never married, never old, never addicted. He knew the pull of hunger, of comfort and of pride, as the temptations in the wilderness show (Matthew 4:1–11), and he knew loneliness, betrayal and the desire to escape suffering in Gethsemane. There was one difference. Our temptations often rise from desires already disordered within us (James 1:14); his came from outside, never from a sinful heart. He felt them in full; he never fed them. So whatever form your temptation takes, you can bring it to him without shame. He will not be shocked, and he knows the way through.

Does his sympathy mean he excuses my sin? No. He sympathises with your weakness, not with your sin; he feels with you in the struggle, and he is on your side against the sin. That is why his sympathy is so strong a help. A friend who excuses you leaves you where you are; a friend who understands and also hates what is destroying you will help you fight it. Jesus is both merciful and faithful (2:17). Come to him expecting tenderness, and expecting him to lead you out.

In a sentence. So, since we have a great high priest who has gone through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us keep a firm grip on the faith we confess. For our high priest is not one who cannot feel for us in our weaknesses; he has been tested in every way, just as we are, yet he never sinned.

On a Tuesday. Name your particular weakness this week: the tiredness that makes you short-tempered, the fear that makes you avoid things, the temptation that keeps coming back. Tell Jesus about it in plain words, as you would a friend who has been through the same thing. Then hold fast your confession by saying, out loud if you can, who he is: Jesus, the Son of God, my great high priest.

For worship. He has passed through the heavens and sits enthroned in the presence of God, and he has not forgotten what it is to be weak. The Son of God knows hunger, exhaustion, grief and the full weight of temptation, carried all the way to the end without once giving way. He is the most exalted being in the universe and the most understanding friend a sinner has ever had. In heaven there is a man who feels for us, and he is God.

verseByVerse.quote: Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need.

Let us then with confidence draw near. Everything in the letter so far has been building to this sentence, and everything after it will be building on it. “Draw near” (proserchōmetha) is present tense: keep coming. It is priestly language (Leviticus 9:7; 21:17). In the Old Testament it is what priests do, and what nobody else may do. The ordinary Israelite stood at a distance; only the high priest could approach God’s presence, once a year, with blood, and the penalty for approaching wrongly was death. That the whole congregation is now told to draw near, at any time, is a revolution stated in two words.

With confidence. “Confidence” (parrēsia) is boldness, freedom of speech, openness, and originally the right of a free citizen to speak openly in the assembly. It is the opposite of the slave’s silence and the suppliant’s hesitation. We are to come with our mouths open. Not arrogance, but freedom to come without fear, because of our high priest (10:19–22).

Exposed, and invited closer. And consider where that instruction sits. Three verses earlier we were told that nothing is hidden and everything is laid bare before the eyes of the one to whom we must give account. The natural response to being exposed is to cover up and withdraw. The writer says the opposite: precisely because you are seen through, come closer, and come speaking freely. There is nothing left to hide, which turns out to be a liberty rather than a terror.

To the throne of grace. It is a throne: not an altar, not a bench, not a counter. Real authority sits on it, God’s royal seat, and a throne is the last place a guilty man would ordinarily approach. For sinners, God’s throne would be a throne of judgement. But because of our high priest, it is a throne of grace (tō thronō tēs charitos), where grace is dispensed, which is a combination the ancient world had no category for: power that gives rather than power that takes. Behind the phrase stands the mercy seat, the lid of the ark of the covenant, God’s throne in the Most Holy Place, where he said he would meet with his people (Exodus 25:22). It was a throne with blood on it.

That we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need. The two are distinct, and both are wanted. Mercy (eleos) is not getting what we deserve: pity, forgiveness for our failures and sins. It looks backward. Grace is getting what we do not deserve: strength for what comes next. It looks forward. A person who comes to this throne needs pardon for what is behind and power for what is ahead, and both are on offer at the same seat. “In time of need” (eukairon) is one word, meaning well-timed, at the right moment: grace that arrives exactly when needed. And “help” (boētheia) is the same word as 2:18, running to aid at a cry. The help does not arrive in advance to be stockpiled. It arrives when it is needed, which requires that we keep coming, and that is the whole point of a throne you are invited to approach with your mouth open.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we should come casually or irreverently. We come with confidence, but to a throne. Nor does it mean we need saints, priests or Mary to approach for us; Christ is our only and sufficient high priest (1 Timothy 2:5).

How can I come boldly when I have just sinned again? By remembering that your confidence was never in your record. You do not come because you have done well this week; you come because your high priest has passed through the heavens with his own blood, and he is the reason the throne is a throne of grace. The moment after a sin is exactly the time of need this verse is talking about. Do not wait until you feel worthy, or punish yourself first to earn the right to pray. Come at once, name the sin, receive the mercy, and ask for the grace to do differently next time. The longer you stay away, the harder you will find it to come.

What if I do not know what to pray? Come anyway, and say so. You can bring a groan, a single sentence, or a name. The Spirit helps us in our weakness and intercedes for us when we do not know what to pray for as we ought (Romans 8:26), and the high priest at the throne already knows your need better than you do. Use the Psalms when you have no words; pray the Lord’s Prayer slowly; tell God plainly that you are tired and need help. Boldness is not eloquence. It is coming in.

In a sentence. So let us come boldly to the throne where grace is given, so that we may receive mercy and find grace to help us at the moment we need it.

On a Tuesday. Come to God in prayer right now, boldly, through Jesus. Ask in two parts: mercy for one specific thing you have done, and grace for one specific thing you face today. Then do it again at the moment of need: before the hard conversation, in the middle of the temptation, when the news comes. Make the throne of grace the first place you run, not the last.

For worship. In the old tabernacle a curtain hung between the people and the throne of God, and one man, once a year, went trembling through it with blood. Now the curtain is torn, the high priest has gone through the heavens with his own blood, and the throne he sits beside is a throne of grace. The King of the universe has opened his court to beggars, and tells them to come boldly and speak freely. Mercy for everything behind us, grace for everything ahead, and a welcome at the very centre of heaven, because Jesus the Son of God is there, and he is ours.
