8.title: A Better Covenant: Written on the Heart
8.overview:
Chapter 8 caps the argument about priesthood: a better Priest ministers in a better sanctuary under a better covenant. The “main point” (v. 1) is that our high priest is seated at God’s right hand in heaven, serving in the true tent. The earthly tabernacle Moses built was a copy and shadow of the heavenly reality (Exodus 25:40).

The better covenant is then proved by the longest Old Testament quotation in the New: Jeremiah 31:31–34. Written while the temple stood, it promised a new covenant unlike Sinai: law written on the heart, everyone knowing God, and “I will remember their sins no more”. By calling it “new”, God made the old obsolete, and “what is growing old is ready to vanish away”. There is nothing to go back to.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — A Minister in the True Tent
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The writer states his main point: we have a high priest who sits at the right hand of God’s majesty in heaven, ministering in the real sanctuary, the true tent set up by the Lord rather than by human hands. Every high priest exists to offer something, so Christ too must have an offering. If he were on earth he would not be a priest at all, since priests already serve there according to the law; but their sanctuary is only a copy and shadow of the heavenly one, as God warned Moses when he told him to build everything according to the pattern shown on the mountain. Christ’s ministry is as much better than theirs as the covenant he mediates is better, founded on better promises.
verseByVerse.theology:
Copy, Shadow, and the Pattern on the Mountain

The earthly tent was a copy of what Moses was shown. Christ ministers in the true tent, and the covenant he mediates is better because it rests on better promises.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Readers grieving the loss of the temple had not been shut out of the sanctuary.

Now: They had been let into the one the sanctuary pictured, where their high priest is seated.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the point in what we are saying is this: we have such a high priest, one who is seated at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in heaven, a minister in the holy places, in the true tent that the Lord set up, not man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the point in what we are saying is this: we have such a high priest, one who is seated at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in heaven, a minister in the holy places, in the true tent that the Lord set up, not man.

Meaning first. Hebrews 8 sums up the argument so far and introduces the new covenant. The main point is this: we have a high priest seated at God’s right hand, who serves in the true sanctuary in heaven, set up by the Lord, not by human hands (vv. 1–2). Every high priest offers gifts and sacrifices, so Christ also has something to offer; but if he were on earth he would not be a priest at all, since the Levitical priests serve there in a sanctuary that is only a copy and shadow of the heavenly one, built according to the pattern God showed Moses on the mountain (vv. 3–5). Christ’s ministry is far better, as the covenant he mediates is better, founded on better promises (v. 6). The proof is that God himself, through Jeremiah, found fault with the first covenant and promised a new one (vv. 7–12): not like the covenant with the fathers at the exodus, which they broke, but one in which God writes his laws on their hearts, is their God and they his people, in which all of them, from least to greatest, know him personally, and in which he forgives their sins and remembers them no more. By calling it “new,” God has made the first one old, and what is old is about to disappear (v. 13).

Now the point in what we are saying is this. Key words. “Point” (kephalaion, main thing, head, summary, chief point). The author steps back to state the heart of the argument.

We have such a high priest. Key words. “We have” (echomen): present possession. Not a theory, but a reality the readers already have. Why return to the old priesthood?

One who is seated at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in heaven. Key words. “Seated” (ekathisen): his work is finished (1:3; 10:12). “Right hand of the throne”: the place of supreme authority. No Levitical priest ever sat in God’s presence, still less on a throne.

A minister in the holy places. Key words. “Minister” (leitourgos, public servant, one who performs priestly service; our word “liturgy”). “Holy places” (tōn hagiōn, the sanctuary, the Most Holy Place): the very presence of God.

In the true tent that the Lord set up, not man. Key words. “True” (alēthinēs, real, genuine, the original as opposed to the copy). “Tent” (skēnēs, tabernacle). The tabernacle Moses built was a real tent but a copy; the true tabernacle is the heavenly reality, God’s own presence. “Set up” (epēxen, pitched, as one pitches a tent). By the Lord, not by human hands (9:11, 24).

What it does not mean. It does not mean heaven literally contains a tent made of heavenly materials. The language describes the heavenly reality of God’s presence, which the tabernacle pictured. Nor does “true” mean the earthly tabernacle was false; it was a true copy, but only a copy.

In a sentence. The main point of what we are saying is this: we do have such a high priest, one who sat down at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in heaven, and who serves in the sanctuary, the true tabernacle set up by the Lord, not by any human being.

For worship. Lift your eyes to heaven: your High Priest is there now, enthroned, serving for you in God’s very presence.

verseByVerse.quote: For every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices; thus it is necessary for this priest also to have something to offer. Now if he were on earth, he would not be a priest at all, since there are priests who offer gifts according to the law. They serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly things. For when Moses was about to erect the tent, he was instructed by God, saying, “See that you make everything according to the pattern that was shown you on the mountain.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
For every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices; thus it is necessary for this priest also to have something to offer. Now if he were on earth, he would not be a priest at all, since there are priests who offer gifts according to the law. They serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly things. For when Moses was about to erect the tent, he was instructed by God, saying, “See that you make everything according to the pattern that was shown you on the mountain.”

For every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices. Key words. As in 5:1. Offering is the essence of priesthood.

Thus it is necessary for this priest also to have something to offer. Key words. “Something to offer” (ti kai touton ho prosenenkē). The aorist tense (“offer”) points to a single offering: himself (7:27; 9:14).

Now if he were on earth, he would not be a priest at all. Key words. On earth, the priesthood belonged to Levi’s line; Jesus was from Judah (7:13–14). His priestly ministry is exercised in heaven. His sacrifice was made on earth, at the cross; but he entered heaven with it and serves there.

Since there are priests who offer gifts according to the law. Key words. “There are” (present tense): the temple was still standing and its priests still offering, which suggests the letter was written before AD 70.

They serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly things. Key words. “Copy” (hypodeigmati, example, sketch, model). “Shadow” (skia, outline, a shadow cast by a real object). A shadow shows the shape of something real but has no substance of its own (10:1; Colossians 2:17). The tabernacle and its ritual were God-given sketches of heavenly realities, pointing to Christ.

For when Moses was about to erect the tent, he was instructed by God. Key words. “Instructed” (kechrēmatistai, warned, divinely directed).

See that you make everything according to the pattern that was shown you on the mountain. Key words. From Exodus 25:40. “Pattern” (typon, model, design, type). God showed Moses a pattern on Mount Sinai. The earthly tabernacle was copied from a heavenly original. Everything in it had to be exact, because it was a picture of something greater.

Where Christians differ: will the temple and its sacrifices be restored? Some dispensationalists expect a rebuilt temple in Jerusalem with renewed animal sacrifices during a future millennium, often as memorials. Verdict: Hebrews teaches that the earthly sanctuary and its sacrifices were shadows, now fulfilled and made obsolete in Christ (v. 13; 10:1–18). To return to them would be to go back from the reality to the shadow, the very thing the letter warns against. The true temple now is Christ himself and his people (John 2:19–21; Ephesians 2:19–22), and the future hope is the new creation where God and the Lamb are the temple (Revelation 21:22).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the tabernacle was unimportant. It was designed by God himself. But its importance lay in what it pointed to.

In a sentence. Every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices, so this one too had to have something to offer. If he were on earth, he would not be a priest at all, because there are already priests who offer the gifts the law prescribes. They serve in a sanctuary that is a copy and shadow of what is in heaven. That is why Moses was warned when he was about to build the tabernacle: “See to it that you make everything according to the pattern shown you on the mountain.”

For worship. Thank God that you do not live among shadows but in the light of the reality, Christ himself.

verseByVerse.quote: But as it is, Christ has obtained a ministry that is as much more excellent than the old as the covenant he mediates is better, since it is enacted on better promises.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But as it is, Christ has obtained a ministry that is as much more excellent than the old as the covenant he mediates is better, since it is enacted on better promises.

But as it is, Christ has obtained a ministry that is as much more excellent than the old. Key words. “As it is” (nyn de, but now): in reality. “Obtained” (tetychen, has attained, perfect tense). “Ministry” (leitourgias, priestly service). “More excellent” (diaphorōteras), the same word used of his name in 1:4.

As the covenant he mediates is better. Key words. “Covenant” (diathēkēs): a binding arrangement, initiated by God, in which he commits himself to his people and they to him. “Mediates” (mesitēs, mediator, go-between), as in 1 Timothy 2:5. Moses mediated the old covenant at Sinai (Galatians 3:19); Christ mediates the new (9:15; 12:24). “Better” (kreittonos).

Since it is enacted on better promises. Key words. “Enacted” (nenomothetētai, legally established, legislated). “Better promises”: the promises of verses 10–12: an inward law, a personal relationship with God, universal knowledge of God among his people, and complete forgiveness. The old covenant had promises too, but they were conditional on Israel’s obedience, which failed. The new covenant promises are unconditionally guaranteed by Christ (7:22).

What it does not mean. It does not mean God changed his mind about his people. The new covenant fulfils what the old covenant always pointed toward, and continues the promises God made to Abraham (Galatians 3:15–18).

In a sentence. But in fact the ministry Jesus has received is far greater than theirs, just as the covenant he mediates is better than the old one, because it is founded on better promises.

For worship. Thank Christ, the mediator of the new covenant, for its better promises, all of which are yes in him (2 Corinthians 1:20).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–13 — The New Covenant Promised by Jeremiah
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: If the first covenant had been without fault, there would have been no need for a second. But God found fault with the people and promised through Jeremiah a new covenant, unlike the one at Sinai which they broke. He would write his laws on their hearts, be their God, and all would know him, from the least to the greatest, for he would forgive their sins and remember them no more. By calling it new, he made the first obsolete, and what is obsolete will soon disappear.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Verbs Have Changed Hands

In Jeremiah's promise God says “I will”: the law written on the heart, knowledge of God for all, and sins remembered no more.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: God found fault with the people, not with the covenant.

Now: God does not forget; he has resolved never to act toward his people on the basis of their sins.

verseByVerse.quote: For if that first covenant had been faultless, there would have been no occasion to look for a second. For he finds fault with them when he says: “Behold, the days are coming, declares the Lord, when I will establish a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah, not like the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt. For they did not continue in my covenant, and so I showed no concern for them, declares the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if that first covenant had been faultless, there would have been no occasion to look for a second. For he finds fault with them when he says: “Behold, the days are coming, declares the Lord, when I will establish a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah, not like the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt. For they did not continue in my covenant, and so I showed no concern for them, declares the Lord.

For if that first covenant had been faultless. Key words. “Faultless” (amemptos, blameless, without defect). The same logic as 7:11: if the old had been sufficient, no new one would be needed.

There would have been no occasion to look for a second. Key words. “Occasion” (topos, place, room). There would be no room for a second.

For he finds fault with them when he says. Key words. “Finds fault” (memphomenos, blames). “With them”: with the people. The fault was not in God’s law but in the people who broke it (Romans 8:3). The old covenant had no power to change hearts.

Behold, the days are coming, declares the Lord. Key words. The longest Old Testament quotation in the New Testament runs from here to verse 12. It is Jeremiah 31:31–34, written around 600 BC, as Judah faced exile because of its covenant-breaking. God promised a new beginning.

When I will establish a new covenant. Key words. “Establish” (syntelesō, accomplish, bring to completion). “New” (kainēn, new in quality, fresh, not merely recent). God would make it; it is entirely his initiative.

With the house of Israel and with the house of Judah. Key words. The whole of God’s people, reunited (the kingdom had divided after Solomon). In the New Testament, the new covenant is fulfilled in Christ for the church, the true Israel, made up of believing Jews and Gentiles (Luke 22:20; 1 Corinthians 11:25; 2 Corinthians 3:6; Galatians 6:16).

Not like the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt. Key words. The Sinai covenant. “Took them by the hand”: a tender image of God leading his people like a father with a child (Hosea 11:1–4).

For they did not continue in my covenant. Key words. “Continue” (enemeinan, remain). Israel broke the covenant again and again, beginning with the golden calf (Exodus 32).

And so I showed no concern for them, declares the Lord. Key words. “Showed no concern” (ēmelēsa, disregarded, neglected), following the Greek translation; the Hebrew reads “though I was their husband.” Either way, the broken covenant brought judgement.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God has abandoned ethnic Israel. Paul teaches that God still has a purpose for Israel, and that many Jews will be brought into the new covenant through faith in Christ (Romans 11:25–29). But the new covenant is entered only through Christ.

In a sentence. If the first covenant had been without fault, no one would have looked for a second. But God found fault with the people and said: “The days are coming, says the Lord, when I will make a new covenant with the people of Israel and the people of Judah. It will not be like the covenant I made with their ancestors when I took them by the hand to lead them out of Egypt, because they did not stay faithful to my covenant, and so I turned away from them, says the Lord.

For worship. Thank God that when his people failed, he did not give up but promised something new and better.
verseByVerse.note: The longest Old Testament quotation in the New Testament runs from v. 8 to v. 12.

verseByVerse.quote: For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the Lord: I will put my laws into their minds, and write them on their hearts, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people. And they shall not teach, each one his neighbor and each one his brother, saying, ’Know the Lord,’ for they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the Lord: I will put my laws into their minds, and write them on their hearts, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people. And they shall not teach, each one his neighbor and each one his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord,’ for they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest.

For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the Lord. Key words. Now the content of the new covenant: four great promises.

I will put my laws into their minds, and write them on their hearts. Key words. The first promise: inward transformation. Under the old covenant, the law was written on tablets of stone (Exodus 31:18), outside the people. In the new covenant, God writes his law on the heart, so that his people want to obey him (Ezekiel 36:26–27; 2 Corinthians 3:3). This is regeneration: a new heart. The law is not abolished but internalised.

And I will be their God, and they shall be my people. Key words. The second promise: relationship. The covenant formula found throughout Scripture (Genesis 17:7; Exodus 6:7; Leviticus 26:12; Revelation 21:3). God gives himself to his people, and takes them as his own.

And they shall not teach, each one his neighbor and each one his brother, saying, Know the Lord. Key words. The third promise: universal personal knowledge of God among his people. Under the old covenant, people were born into the covenant community and then had to be urged to know the Lord; many never did.

For they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest. Key words. “Know” (eidēsousin): not just knowledge about God, but personal, saving knowledge (John 17:3). Every member of the new covenant knows God. There is no mediating priestly class; every believer has direct access. This does not mean teaching is unnecessary in the church (Ephesians 4:11); it means every member truly knows God.

Where Christians differ: who belongs to the new covenant? Paedobaptists see the new covenant, like the old, as including believers and their children, and so baptise infants as covenant members. Verdict: One of the key differences between the old and new covenants is that all members of the new covenant know the Lord personally, from the least to the greatest, and have the law written on their hearts. The old covenant community was mixed, including many who did not know God; the new covenant community, properly understood, consists of those who have been regenerated. This is why baptism, the sign of the new covenant, belongs to those who profess faith. This credobaptist conclusion is held charitably toward paedobaptist brothers, who agree that only the regenerate are truly saved but understand the visible covenant community differently.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every person who attends church is regenerate; the visible church still contains false professors (6:4–6). But the new covenant itself, in its true membership, consists of those who know the Lord.

In a sentence. This is the covenant I will make with the people of Israel after that time, says the Lord: I will put my laws in their minds and write them on their hearts. I will be their God, and they will be my people. No longer will they teach their neighbours, or say to one another, ‘Know the Lord,’ because they will all know me, from the least of them to the greatest.

For worship. Thank God that he has written his law on your heart and that you know him personally. Ask him to deepen that knowledge today.

verseByVerse.quote: For I will be merciful toward their iniquities, and I will remember their sins no more.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I will be merciful toward their iniquities, and I will remember their sins no more.”

For I will be merciful toward their iniquities. Key words. The fourth promise, and the foundation of the others: complete forgiveness. “For” indicates that forgiveness is the basis of everything else. “Merciful” (hileōs, propitious, gracious), related to “propitiation” (2:17). God will be favourable toward his people because their sins have been atoned for. “Iniquities” (adikiais, wrongs, unrighteous deeds).

And I will remember their sins no more. Key words. “Remember no more” (ou mē mnēsthō eti, a strong double negative: I will certainly never again remember). God does not forget in the sense of losing information; he chooses not to hold sins against his people, never to bring them up again, never to punish them (Psalm 103:12; Isaiah 43:25; Micah 7:19). Under the old covenant, the annual Day of Atonement was a reminder of sins year by year (10:3). Under the new, sins are completely and permanently forgiven (10:17–18).

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers never experience the consequences of sin in this life, or that God never disciplines them (12:5–11). It means the guilt and condemnation are gone forever.

In a sentence. For I will show mercy for their wrongdoing, and I will never again remember their sins.”

For worship. If your past sins haunt you, hear God’s promise: he remembers them no more. Rest in that forgiveness today.

verseByVerse.quote: In speaking of a new covenant, he makes the first one obsolete. And what is becoming obsolete and growing old is ready to vanish away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In speaking of a new covenant, he makes the first one obsolete. And what is becoming obsolete and growing old is ready to vanish away.

In speaking of a new covenant, he makes the first one obsolete. Key words. “Makes obsolete” (pepalaiōken, has made old, perfect tense: declared old and remaining so). The very word “new” in Jeremiah’s prophecy shows that the old covenant was always meant to be temporary. When God spoke of a new one, six centuries before Christ, he already marked the old one as old.

And what is becoming obsolete and growing old. Key words. “Becoming obsolete” (palaioumenon, being made old). “Growing old” (gēraskon, ageing, as a person grows old and weak).

Is ready to vanish away. Key words. “Ready” (engys, near). “Vanish away” (aphanismou, disappearance, destruction). When this letter was written, the temple was still standing, but the old system was near its end. Within a few years, in AD 70, the Romans destroyed the temple, and the sacrifices ceased forever. God himself brought the shadow to an end once the reality had come.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Old Testament Scriptures are obsolete. They are God’s word, and they testify to Christ. What has become obsolete is the old covenant as a system: its priesthood, sacrifices and ceremonial law.

In a sentence. By calling this covenant “new,” God has made the first one old; and whatever is old and ageing will soon disappear.

On a Tuesday. Are you holding onto old ways of approaching God: rituals, merit, a sense that you must earn your place? Let them go. Live in the new covenant.

8.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the point in what we are saying is this: we have such a high priest, one who is seated at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in heaven,<sup>2</sup>a minister in the holy places, in the true tent that the Lord set up, not man.<sup>3</sup>For every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices; thus it is necessary for this priest also to have something to offer.<sup>4</sup>Now if he were on earth, he would not be a priest at all, since there are priests who offer gifts according to the law.<sup>5</sup>They serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly things. For when Moses was about to erect the tent, he was instructed by God, saying, “See that you make everything according to the pattern that was shown you on the mountain.”<sup>6</sup>But as it is, Christ has obtained a ministry that is as much more excellent than the old as the covenant he mediates is better, since it is enacted on better promises.<sup>7</sup>For if that first covenant had been faultless, there would have been no occasion to look for a second.<sup>8</sup>For he finds fault with them when he says: “Behold, the days are coming, declares the Lord, when I will establish a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah,<sup>9</sup>not like the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt. For they did not continue in my covenant, and so I showed no concern for them, declares the Lord.<sup>10</sup>For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the Lord: I will put my laws into their minds, and write them on their hearts, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.<sup>11</sup>And they shall not teach, each one his neighbor and each one his brother, saying, ’Know the Lord,’ for they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest.<sup>12</sup>For I will be merciful toward their iniquities, and I will remember their sins no more.”<sup>13</sup>In speaking of a new covenant, he makes the first one obsolete. And what is becoming obsolete and growing old is ready to vanish away.

9.title: The Blood of Christ: Once for All Into the Holy Place
9.overview:
Chapter 9 is the heart of Hebrews’ teaching on atonement. The tabernacle’s design was itself a sermon about access to God: restricted, mediated, temporary. Priests entered the outer room daily; only the high priest entered the inner room, once a year, never without blood. By this the Spirit was saying: the way in is not yet open.

When Christ came, he entered not a tent of cloth but heaven itself, not with animals’ blood but with his own, once for all, securing eternal redemption. His blood cleanses not only the body but the conscience, freeing us from dead works to serve the living God. And as we die once and then face judgment, so Christ, offered once to bear the sins of many, will appear a second time, not to deal with sin, but to save those who eagerly wait for him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — The Closed Door, and the Blood That Opened It
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The first covenant had a sanctuary: an outer Holy Place with lampstand and bread, and behind a curtain the Most Holy Place with the ark, the manna, Aaron’s staff, the tablets and the mercy seat. Priests went into the outer room daily, but only the high priest went into the inner room, once a year, with blood for his own sins and the people’s. The Spirit was showing that the way in was not yet open; those sacrifices could not cleanse the conscience. But Christ entered the true sanctuary once for all with his own blood. If animals’ blood purified the body, how much more will Christ’s blood, offered through the eternal Spirit, cleanse our conscience to serve the living God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Architecture That Preached

By the tabernacle's design the Holy Spirit was saying not yet: one man, one day a year, never without blood. Its sacrifices could not perfect the conscience; the blood of Christ does.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The ark held manna, Aaron's staff and the tablets, with the mercy seat over them.

Now: A cleansed conscience is set free from dead works to serve the living God.

verseByVerse.quote: Now even the first covenant had regulations for worship and an earthly place of holiness. For a tent was prepared, the first section, in which were the lampstand and the table and the bread of the Presence. It is called the Holy Place. Behind the second curtain was a second section called the Most Holy Place, having the golden altar of incense and the ark of the covenant covered on all sides with gold, in which was a golden urn holding the manna, and Aaron’s staff that budded, and the tablets of the covenant. Above it were the cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy seat. Of these things we cannot now speak in detail.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now even the first covenant had regulations for worship and an earthly place of holiness. For a tent was prepared, the first section, in which were the lampstand and the table and the bread of the Presence. It is called the Holy Place. Behind the second curtain was a second section called the Most Holy Place, having the golden altar of incense and the ark of the covenant covered on all sides with gold, in which was a golden urn holding the manna, and Aaron’s staff that budded, and the tablets of the covenant. Above it were the cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy seat. Of these things we cannot now speak in detail.

Meaning first. Hebrews 9 compares the worship of the old covenant with Christ’s work, showing how the old system pictured and pointed to his once-for-all sacrifice. First, the earthly tabernacle (vv. 1–5): an outer room, the Holy Place, with the lampstand, table and bread; and behind a curtain an inner room, the Most Holy Place, with the ark of the covenant and the mercy seat overshadowed by cherubim. Priests went into the outer room daily, but only the high priest entered the inner room, once a year, with blood for his own sins and the people’s (vv. 6–7). The Holy Spirit was showing by this that the way into God’s presence was not yet open while the old tabernacle stood, and its sacrifices could not cleanse the conscience; they were external rules until the time of reformation (vv. 8–10). But Christ has come as high priest, entering the true sanctuary once for all with his own blood, securing eternal redemption (vv. 11–12). If animal blood could make people outwardly clean, how much more will Christ’s blood, offered through the eternal Spirit, cleanse our consciences to serve the living God (vv. 13–14). So he is the mediator of a new covenant, whose death redeems from sins and secures the eternal inheritance (v. 15). A covenant, like a will, requires death; even the first covenant was inaugurated with blood, for without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness (vv. 16–22). The heavenly realities needed better sacrifices: Christ entered heaven itself, not repeatedly but once, at the climax of history, to put away sin by sacrificing himself (vv. 23–26). As people die once and then face judgement, so Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many, and will appear a second time, not to deal with sin, but to bring salvation to those waiting for him (vv. 27–28).

Now even the first covenant had regulations for worship and an earthly place of holiness. Key words. “Regulations” (dikaiōmata, ordinances, requirements). “Worship” (latreias, service, religious ritual). “Earthly” (kosmikon, belonging to this world). The first covenant had its own God-given system, but it was of this world, as opposed to the heavenly sanctuary.

For a tent was prepared, the first section. Key words. “Tent” (skēnē, tabernacle): the portable sanctuary built in the wilderness (Exodus 25–40), not the later temple. The author always refers to the tabernacle, the original pattern.

In which were the lampstand and the table and the bread of the Presence. Key words. The lampstand (lychnia, the golden menorah with seven lamps, Exodus 25:31–40), the table (Exodus 25:23–30), and the “bread of the Presence” (twelve loaves set before God each week, representing the twelve tribes, Leviticus 24:5–9). They spoke of light, provision and fellowship in God’s presence, fulfilled in Christ, the light of the world and the bread of life (John 8:12; 6:35).

It is called the Holy Place. Key words. “Holy Place” (Hagia). The outer room, about thirty feet long.

Behind the second curtain was a second section called the Most Holy Place. Key words. “Second curtain”: the thick veil dividing the two rooms (Exodus 26:31–33). The first curtain was at the tabernacle entrance. “Most Holy Place” (Hagia Hagiōn, Holy of Holies): a perfect cube, about fifteen feet each way, where God’s presence dwelt above the ark.

Having the golden altar of incense. Key words. “Golden altar of incense” (chrysoun thymiatērion): either the altar of incense or a golden censer. The altar of incense actually stood in the Holy Place, just in front of the curtain (Exodus 30:1–6). The author says the Most Holy Place “had” it: it belonged to the inner room in function, because the incense from it was taken into the Most Holy Place on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:12–13), and 1 Kings 6:22 says the altar “belonged to the inner sanctuary.” Some take the word as the golden censer used by the high priest. Either way, no contradiction.

And the ark of the covenant covered on all sides with gold. Key words. “Ark” (kibōton, chest, box): a wooden chest about four feet long, overlaid with gold (Exodus 25:10–22).

In which was a golden urn holding the manna, and Aaron’s staff that budded, and the tablets of the covenant. Key words. Three reminders: the manna God provided in the wilderness (Exodus 16:32–34); Aaron’s staff, which budded to prove God’s choice of Aaron as priest (Numbers 17:1–11); and the stone tablets of the Ten Commandments (Exodus 25:16; Deuteronomy 10:1–5). By Solomon’s time, only the tablets remained (1 Kings 8:9). Each pointed to Christ: the bread from heaven, the chosen priest who rose to life, and the one who fulfils the law.

Above it were the cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy seat. Key words. “Cherubim” (cheroubin): two golden angelic figures facing each other with wings outspread over the ark. “Of glory”: associated with God’s glory, which dwelt between them (Exodus 25:22; Numbers 7:89). “Mercy seat” (hilastērion, place of propitiation, atonement cover): the golden lid of the ark, where blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:14–15). The same word Paul uses of Christ in Romans 3:25: Christ is our mercy seat, the place where God’s wrath is turned away. Between God’s presence above and the broken law below lay the blood-sprinkled cover.

Of these things we cannot now speak in detail. Key words. The author could say much more about each item, but his focus is the Day of Atonement and its meaning.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every detail of the tabernacle has a hidden allegorical meaning. Interpreters should follow the New Testament’s lead rather than inventing symbolism. But the whole structure did point to Christ.

In a sentence. The first covenant had rules for worship and a sanctuary on earth. A tabernacle was set up. In its first room were the lampstand, the table and the consecrated bread; this was called the Holy Place. Behind the second curtain was a room called the Most Holy Place, which had the golden altar of incense and the gold-covered ark of the covenant. The ark contained a gold jar of manna, Aaron’s staff that had budded, and the stone tablets of the covenant. Above the ark were the cherubim of the Glory, overshadowing the atonement cover. But we cannot discuss these things in detail now.

For worship. Thank God that Christ is your mercy seat, where his blood covers the law you broke and God meets you in grace.

verseByVerse.quote: These preparations having thus been made, the priests go regularly into the first section, performing their ritual duties, but into the second only the high priest goes, and he but once a year, and not without taking blood, which he offers for himself and for the unintentional sins of the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These preparations having thus been made, the priests go regularly into the first section, performing their ritual duties, but into the second only the high priest goes, and he but once a year, and not without taking blood, which he offers for himself and for the unintentional sins of the people.

These preparations having thus been made, the priests go regularly into the first section. Key words. “Regularly” (dia pantos, continually). Priests entered the Holy Place every day, morning and evening, to tend the lamps, burn incense, and change the bread weekly (Exodus 27:20–21; 30:7–8). Constant activity, never finished.

Performing their ritual duties. Key words. “Ritual duties” (latreias epitelountes, completing services).

But into the second only the high priest goes. Key words. Only one man in the whole nation.

And he but once a year. Key words. On the Day of Atonement, Yom Kippur, the tenth day of the seventh month (Leviticus 16:29–34; 23:26–32). Even then, he entered more than once that day (incense, then blood for himself, then blood for the people), but only on that one day of the year.

And not without taking blood. Key words. Never without blood. Without a death, no approach to God was possible. The point anticipates verse 22.

Which he offers for himself and for the unintentional sins of the people. Key words. First for himself, a bull (Leviticus 16:11); then for the people, a goat (16:15). “Unintentional sins” (agnoēmatōn, sins of ignorance). The sacrifices covered sins of weakness and ignorance (5:2; Numbers 15:22–31), not deliberate, defiant rebellion.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only sins of ignorance can be forgiven today. Christ’s sacrifice cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7, 9), including deliberate sins repented of, as David’s were (Psalm 51). What cannot be forgiven is the persistent rejection of the only sacrifice (10:26).

In a sentence. When everything had been arranged like this, the priests went regularly into the outer room to carry out their ministry. But only the high priest entered the inner room, and only once a year, and never without blood, which he offered for himself and for the sins the people had committed in ignorance.

For worship. Imagine standing outside, never allowed in. Then thank God that through Christ you may come into his presence every day.

verseByVerse.quote: By this the Holy Spirit indicates that the way into the holy places is not yet opened as long as the first section is still standing (which is symbolic for the present age). According to this arrangement, gifts and sacrifices are offered that cannot perfect the conscience of the worshiper, but deal only with food and drink and various washings, regulations for the body imposed until the time of reformation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By this the Holy Spirit indicates that the way into the holy places is not yet opened as long as the first section is still standing (which is symbolic for the present age). According to this arrangement, gifts and sacrifices are offered that cannot perfect the conscience of the worshiper, but deal only with food and drink and various washings, regulations for the body imposed until the time of reformation.

By this the Holy Spirit indicates. Key words. “Indicates” (dēlountos, makes clear, shows). The Holy Spirit, who inspired the design of the tabernacle and its record in Scripture, was teaching something through its very structure.

That the way into the holy places is not yet opened. Key words. “Way” (hodon, road, path). “Holy places”: God’s true presence. As long as the curtain stood and only the high priest could pass once a year, the message was clear: the way to God is not yet open. At Jesus’ death, the temple curtain was torn in two from top to bottom (Matthew 27:51; Mark 15:38). The way is now open (10:19–20).

As long as the first section is still standing. Key words. “First section” (prōtēs skēnēs, first tent): the outer room, or perhaps the whole first tabernacle system. As long as that system stood, access was barred.

Which is symbolic for the present age. Key words. “Symbolic” (parabolē, parable, illustration, figure). The tabernacle was a parable for the time then present, the old covenant era.

According to this arrangement, gifts and sacrifices are offered that cannot perfect the conscience of the worshiper. Key words. “Perfect” (teleiōsai, complete, bring to the goal). “Conscience” (syneidēsin, the inner moral awareness of guilt). The deepest problem: the old sacrifices could not remove the inner sense of guilt and give a clear conscience before God (10:1–4). They dealt with outward ritual impurity, not the heart.

But deal only with food and drink and various washings. Key words. Food laws (Leviticus 11), drink offerings and regulations (Numbers 6:3), ritual washings (Leviticus 15; Numbers 19). External matters.

Regulations for the body imposed until the time of reformation. Key words. “Regulations for the body” (dikaiōmata sarkos, ordinances of the flesh): external rules. “Imposed” (epikeimena, laid on, like a burden, Acts 15:10). “Until the time of reformation” (mechri kairou diorthōseos, until the time of setting things straight, of a new order). The new covenant era in Christ. The old rules were always temporary.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the old covenant believers had no forgiveness. They were forgiven through faith in God’s promise, looking forward to what the sacrifices pointed to (11:39–40; Romans 3:25). But the sacrifices themselves could not provide the clear conscience that Christ gives.

In a sentence. The Holy Spirit was showing by this that the way into the Most Holy Place had not yet been opened as long as the first tabernacle was still standing. This is an illustration for that time, showing that the gifts and sacrifices being offered could not clear the conscience of the worshipper. They dealt only with food and drink and various ceremonial washings, external regulations in force until the time when God would set things right.

For worship. Do you have a guilty conscience? Rituals cannot clean it. Bring it to Christ, whose blood does.

verseByVerse.quote: But when Christ appeared as a high priest of the good things that have come, then through the greater and more perfect tent (not made with hands, that is, not of this creation) he entered once for all into the holy places, not by means of the blood of goats and calves but by means of his own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when Christ appeared as a high priest of the good things that have come, then through the greater and more perfect tent (not made with hands, that is, not of this creation) he entered once for all into the holy places, not by means of the blood of goats and calves but by means of his own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption.

But when Christ appeared as a high priest of the good things that have come. Key words. “Appeared” (paragenomenos, arrived, came on the scene). “Good things that have come” (tōn genomenōn agathōn): the blessings of the new covenant, already present. Some manuscripts read “good things to come” (mellontōn), as in 10:1. Either way: real forgiveness, access to God, a clean conscience.

Then through the greater and more perfect tent. Key words. “Greater” (meizonos) and “more perfect” (teleioteras). The heavenly sanctuary.

Not made with hands, that is, not of this creation. Key words. “Not made with hands” (ou cheiropoiētou), a phrase used to contrast human-made shrines with God’s reality (Acts 7:48; Mark 14:58). “Not of this creation”: heavenly, not earthly.

He entered once for all into the holy places. Key words. “Once for all” (ephapax), as in 7:27. Not once a year, but once in all history, never to be repeated. At his ascension, he entered God’s presence (v. 24).

Not by means of the blood of goats and calves but by means of his own blood. Key words. “His own blood”: his life poured out in death. Not animal blood, which could not cleanse (10:4), but the blood of the sinless God-man. Blood signifies life given up in death (Leviticus 17:11).

Thus securing an eternal redemption. Key words. “Securing” (heuramenos, having obtained, found). Aorist: a finished achievement. “Eternal” (aiōnian): unlike the annual atonement, which lasted only a year, Christ’s redemption lasts forever. “Redemption” (lytrōsin, liberation by payment of a ransom). Not a possible redemption, offered to all and secured for none; an actual redemption, obtained and secured for those for whom he died.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ literally carried a vessel of blood into heaven. “By means of his own blood” means on the basis of his completed sacrifice. Nor does it mean his work in heaven completes an unfinished sacrifice; the sacrifice was completed on the cross (John 19:30).

In a sentence. But when Christ came as high priest of the good things that are now here, he went through the greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made by human hands and not part of this created world. He entered the Most Holy Place once for all, not with the blood of goats and calves, but with his own blood, and so obtained a redemption that lasts for ever.

For worship. Thank Christ that he did not merely offer redemption but secured it, eternally. Nothing can undo what his blood has done for you.

verseByVerse.quote: For if the blood of goats and bulls, and the sprinkling of defiled persons with the ashes of a heifer, sanctify for the purification of the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purify our conscience from dead works to serve the living God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if the blood of goats and bulls, and the sprinkling of defiled persons with the ashes of a heifer, sanctify for the purification of the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purify our conscience from dead works to serve the living God.

For if the blood of goats and bulls. Key words. The Day of Atonement sacrifices (Leviticus 16).

And the sprinkling of defiled persons with the ashes of a heifer. Key words. The ashes of a red heifer were mixed with water to cleanse anyone who had become ritually unclean by touching a dead body (Numbers 19). The heifer was burned outside the camp, and its ashes kept for this purpose.

Sanctify for the purification of the flesh. Key words. “Sanctify” (hagiazei, make holy). “Purification of the flesh” (tēn tēs sarkos katharotēta, outward, bodily cleanness). These rites did really restore ritual purity, allowing people to take part in worship again. But only outwardly.

How much more will the blood of Christ. Key words. “How much more” (posō mallon): the argument from lesser to greater. If the shadow worked outwardly, how much more the reality inwardly.

Who through the eternal Spirit offered himself. Key words. “Through the eternal Spirit” (dia pneumatos aiōniou): most likely the Holy Spirit, who empowered Christ throughout his ministry (Luke 4:18; Acts 10:38) and in his self-offering. The whole Trinity is at work: the Son offers himself to the Father through the Spirit. “Eternal”: his sacrifice has eternal value. “Offered himself”: Christ was both priest and sacrifice, offering voluntarily (John 10:17–18).

Without blemish to God. Key words. “Without blemish” (amōmon, spotless, unblemished). Sacrificial animals had to be perfect (Leviticus 22:20–22). Christ was morally perfect, sinless (1 Peter 1:19).

Purify our conscience from dead works. Key words. “Purify” (kathariei, cleanse). “Conscience”: the inner guilt that the old sacrifices could not touch (v. 9). “Dead works” (nekrōn ergōn), as in 6:1: works that lead to death, sins, and perhaps also religious works done to earn favour. Just as touching a dead body defiled a person (Numbers 19), dead works defile the conscience. Christ’s blood cleanses.

To serve the living God. Key words. “Serve” (latreuein, worship, serve as a priest). The purpose of cleansing: to worship and serve. A clean conscience is freed for joyful service. “The living God”: in contrast with dead works.

What it does not mean. It does not mean a believer will never feel guilt. When we sin, we feel it, and we should; but we bring it to Christ, whose blood keeps cleansing (1 John 1:7–9). Nor does it mean we serve in order to be cleansed; we are cleansed in order to serve.

In a sentence. The blood of goats and bulls and the ashes of a heifer sprinkled on those who are ceremonially unclean make them outwardly clean. How much more, then, will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, cleanse our consciences from deeds that lead to death, so that we may serve the living God!

For worship. Let Christ’s blood cleanse your conscience today. Then serve the living God with freedom and joy, not with guilt.
verseByVerse.note: The ashes of a red heifer were mixed with water to cleanse anyone defiled by touching a corpse.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–28 — A Death That Reaches Backward, and a Return Without Sin
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Christ is the mediator of a new covenant, and his death redeems people even from the sins committed under the first covenant, so that those God calls can receive the promised eternal inheritance. A will takes effect only when the one who made it dies, and in the same way the first covenant was inaugurated with blood: Moses sprinkled the book, the people, the tent and its vessels, for under the law almost everything is cleansed with blood, and without shedding of blood there is no forgiveness. The earthly copies were cleansed with animal sacrifices, but the heavenly realities needed better ones. Christ did not enter a man-made sanctuary but heaven itself, to appear before God for us. He did not offer himself repeatedly, as the high priest entered year after year with blood not his own; he appeared once, at the climax of the ages, to put away sin by sacrificing himself. Just as people die once and then face judgement, Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many, and he will appear a second time, not to deal with sin, but to bring salvation to those who are eagerly waiting for him.
verseByVerse.theology:
How the Old Testament Saints Were Saved

Christ's death redeems from transgressions committed under the first covenant. There is one way of salvation, looked forward to and looked back on.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: At Sinai the book and the people were sprinkled with the blood of the covenant.

Now: Christ will appear a second time, not to deal with sin, but to save those eagerly waiting for him.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore he is the mediator of a new covenant, so that those who are called may receive the promised eternal inheritance, since a death has occurred that redeems them from the transgressions committed under the first covenant.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore he is the mediator of a new covenant, so that those who are called may receive the promised eternal inheritance, since a death has occurred that redeems them from the transgressions committed under the first covenant.

Therefore he is the mediator of a new covenant. Key words. “Therefore” (dia touto): because his blood cleanses the conscience (v. 14). “Mediator” (mesitēs), as in 8:6. “New covenant” (diathēkēs kainēs), as promised in Jeremiah 31.

So that those who are called may receive the promised eternal inheritance. Key words. “Those who are called” (hoi keklēmenoi, perfect passive: those who have been called and remain called). God’s effectual call (3:1; Romans 8:28–30). “Receive” (labōsin). “Eternal inheritance” (tēs aiōniou klēronomias): not the land of Canaan, but eternal life, the new creation, God himself (1 Peter 1:4).

Since a death has occurred that redeems them. Key words. “A death” (thanatou genomenou): Christ’s death. “Redeems” (apolytrōsin, release by ransom, redemption).

From the transgressions committed under the first covenant. Key words. Christ’s death reaches back to cover the sins of Old Testament believers, which the animal sacrifices could not truly remove (10:4). Those who trusted God before Christ were forgiven on the basis of what Christ would do (Romans 3:25–26). His death is the ground of all forgiveness, before and after the cross.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ died only for Old Testament sins; it means his death covers them too, along with all the sins of all the called. Nor does “those who are called” mean everyone who hears the gospel invitation; it means those effectually called by God.

In a sentence. That is why Christ is the mediator of a new covenant: so that those God has called may receive the eternal inheritance he promised, now that a death has taken place that sets them free from the sins committed under the first covenant.

For worship. Thank God that you are among the called, and that your eternal inheritance is secured by Christ’s death.

verseByVerse.quote: For where a will is involved, the death of the one who made it must be established. For a will takes effect only at death, since it is not in force as long as the one who made it is alive. Therefore not even the first covenant was inaugurated without blood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For where a will is involved, the death of the one who made it must be established. For a will takes effect only at death, since it is not in force as long as the one who made it is alive. Therefore not even the first covenant was inaugurated without blood.

For where a will is involved. Key words. The Greek word for “covenant” (diathēkē) can also mean a “will,” and the author makes use of both senses here. In everyday Greek, diathēkē usually meant a last will and testament. The author moves from “covenant” to “will” to make a point: an inheritance (v. 15) comes through a will, and a will requires a death.

The death of the one who made it must be established. Key words. “Established” (pheresthai, be brought forward, be proved). Before an inheritance is distributed, the death must be confirmed.

For a will takes effect only at death. Key words. “Takes effect” (bebaia, valid, binding, in force). A will has no power while the testator lives.

Since it is not in force as long as the one who made it is alive. Key words. So the eternal inheritance (v. 15) required Christ’s death. Only when he died did his “will” come into force for his heirs.

Therefore not even the first covenant was inaugurated without blood. Key words. “Inaugurated” (enkekainistai, dedicated, ratified, put into effect). Returning to the covenant sense: the Sinai covenant was ratified by blood (v. 19; Exodus 24:3–8). In ancient covenant-making, a sacrificial death sealed the agreement (Genesis 15:9–18; Jeremiah 34:18–20). Death lies at the heart of both wills and covenants.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God’s covenant is merely a human legal document. The illustration from wills makes a point: a death was necessary. The divine covenant is far greater, and the testator who died is also the one who rose and administers his own will.

In a sentence. In the case of a will, the death of the person who made it must be proved, because a will comes into force only when someone has died; it never takes effect while the one who made it is still alive. That is why even the first covenant was not put into effect without blood.

For worship. Thank Christ that he died so that his will, with all its rich inheritance, might come into force for you.
verseByVerse.note: The Greek word for “covenant” can also mean a “will,” and the writer uses both senses.

verseByVerse.quote: For when every commandment of the law had been declared by Moses to all the people, he took the blood of calves and goats, with water and scarlet wool and hyssop, and sprinkled both the book itself and all the people, saying, “This is the blood of the covenant that God commanded for you.” And in the same way he sprinkled with the blood both the tent and all the vessels used in worship. Indeed, under the law almost everything is purified with blood, and without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For when every commandment of the law had been declared by Moses to all the people, he took the blood of calves and goats, with water and scarlet wool and hyssop, and sprinkled both the book itself and all the people, saying, “This is the blood of the covenant that God commanded for you.” And in the same way he sprinkled with the blood both the tent and all the vessels used in worship. Indeed, under the law almost everything is purified with blood, and without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins.

For when every commandment of the law had been declared by Moses to all the people. Key words. At Sinai, Moses read the Book of the Covenant to the people, and they promised to obey (Exodus 24:3–7).

He took the blood of calves and goats, with water and scarlet wool and hyssop. Key words. Exodus 24 mentions bulls; the author adds details (goats, water, scarlet wool, hyssop) drawn from other sprinkling rituals (Leviticus 14:4–7; Numbers 19:6, 18), perhaps reflecting Jewish tradition or combining related rites. “Hyssop”: a small bushy plant used as a sprinkler (Exodus 12:22; Psalm 51:7).

And sprinkled both the book itself and all the people. Key words. Exodus 24:6–8 mentions sprinkling the altar and the people. The book also is mentioned here. The blood marked both the covenant document and the covenant people as bound together.

Saying, This is the blood of the covenant that God commanded for you. Key words. From Exodus 24:8. Jesus echoed these words at the Last Supper: “This is my blood of the covenant” (Mark 14:24; Matthew 26:28), “the new covenant in my blood” (Luke 22:20). The cup of the Lord’s Supper recalls the ratification of the new covenant by Christ’s blood.

And in the same way he sprinkled with the blood both the tent and all the vessels used in worship. Key words. The tabernacle and its furnishings were consecrated with blood and oil (Exodus 40:9–11; Leviticus 8:15, 19).

Indeed, under the law almost everything is purified with blood. Key words. “Almost” (schedon): some things were purified by water, fire or flour (Leviticus 5:11–13; Numbers 31:22–24). But blood was the main means.

And without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins. Key words. “Shedding of blood” (haimatekchysias, a word perhaps coined by the author: blood-pouring). “Forgiveness” (aphesis, release, cancellation). A fundamental principle: forgiveness requires a death, life given for life (Leviticus 17:11). Sin deserves death (Romans 6:23); forgiveness comes only when a substitute dies in the sinner’s place. This is the logic of penal substitution, which Christ fulfilled.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God is bloodthirsty. It means sin is so serious that it can be dealt with only by death, and God in love provided the death himself, in his Son (Romans 5:8). Nor does it mean animal blood could truly forgive; it pointed to the blood that does (10:4).

In a sentence. When Moses had told all the people every command of the law, he took the blood of calves and goats, together with water, scarlet wool and branches of hyssop, and sprinkled the scroll and all the people. He said, “This is the blood of the covenant, which God has commanded you to keep.” In the same way, he sprinkled with blood the tabernacle and everything used in its worship. In fact, under the law almost everything is made clean with blood, and without the pouring out of blood there is no forgiveness.

For worship. At the next Lord’s Supper, remember: this cup is the new covenant in his blood, poured out for the forgiveness of your sins.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus it was necessary for the copies of the heavenly things to be purified with these rites, but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these. For Christ has entered, not into holy places made with hands, which are copies of the true things, but into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf. Nor was it to offer himself repeatedly, as the high priest enters the holy places every year with blood not his own, for then he would have had to suffer repeatedly since the foundation of the world. But as it is, he has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus it was necessary for the copies of the heavenly things to be purified with these rites, but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these. For Christ has entered, not into holy places made with hands, which are copies of the true things, but into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf. Nor was it to offer himself repeatedly, as the high priest enters the holy places every year with blood not his own, for then he would have had to suffer repeatedly since the foundation of the world. But as it is, he has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself.

Thus it was necessary for the copies of the heavenly things to be purified with these rites. Key words. “Copies” (hypodeigmata), as in 8:5. The earthly tabernacle needed cleansing with animal blood.

But the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these. Key words. Why would heavenly things need cleansing? Not because heaven itself is defiled, but because the approach to God for sinners needed to be opened, and his people (who are his true dwelling) needed cleansing. Some suggest that sinners’ access to heaven had been defiled by sin and needed to be consecrated. “Better sacrifices” (plural, as a general category): Christ’s single sacrifice.

For Christ has entered, not into holy places made with hands, which are copies of the true things. Key words. “Copies” (antitypa, antitypes, corresponding figures). Earthly shrines are copies of the real.

But into heaven itself. Key words. Not a heavenly building, but heaven itself, God’s very presence.

Now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf. Key words. “Appear” (emphanisthēnai, be made visible, present himself). “Now”: at this very moment. Christ stands in God’s presence as our representative (7:25; Romans 8:34; 1 John 2:1).

Nor was it to offer himself repeatedly. Key words. Unlike the high priest’s annual repetition.

As the high priest enters the holy places every year with blood not his own. Key words. “Not his own”: animal blood.

For then he would have had to suffer repeatedly since the foundation of the world. Key words. If his sacrifice needed repeating, he would have had to die again and again, throughout history, since sin began. The absurdity proves the point: one death was enough.

But as it is, he has appeared once for all at the end of the ages. Key words. “Appeared” (pephanerōtai, been manifested, perfect tense). His first coming. “Once for all” (hapax). “End of the ages” (epi synteleia tōn aiōnōn, the consummation, completion of the ages): the climax of history (1:2).

To put away sin by the sacrifice of himself. Key words. “Put away” (athetēsin, abolish, annul, cancel, the same word used of setting aside the commandment, 7:18). Christ annulled sin, cancelling its guilt and power. “By the sacrifice of himself”: not of an animal, but of himself.

What it does not mean. It does not mean heaven was dirty. The cleansing language is about consecrating the way of access for sinners. Nor does Christ’s appearing for us mean the Father is reluctant; the Father sent him (John 3:16).

In a sentence. So it was necessary for the copies of the heavenly things to be purified by these sacrifices, but the heavenly things themselves needed better sacrifices. For Christ did not enter a sanctuary made by human hands, a mere copy of the true one; he entered heaven itself, now to appear for us in God’s presence. Nor did he enter heaven to offer himself again and again, as the high priest enters the Most Holy Place every year with blood that is not his own. Otherwise Christ would have had to suffer many times since the creation of the world. But now he has appeared once for all at the climax of history to do away with sin by sacrificing himself.

For worship. Christ is in God’s presence for you right now. Your sin has been put away by his one sacrifice. Worship him.

verseByVerse.quote: And just as it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment, so Christ, having been offered once to bear the sins of many, will appear a second time, not to deal with sin but to save those who are eagerly waiting for him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And just as it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment, so Christ, having been offered once to bear the sins of many, will appear a second time, not to deal with sin but to save those who are eagerly waiting for him.

And just as it is appointed for man to die once. Key words. “Appointed” (apokeitai, laid up, reserved, destined). “Once” (hapax). Every human being dies once (except those alive at Christ’s return, 1 Corinthians 15:51–52, and Enoch and Elijah). Death is God’s appointment because of sin (Genesis 3:19; Romans 5:12).

And after that comes judgment. Key words. “Judgment” (krisis). After death, every person faces God’s judgement. There is no second chance after death, no reincarnation, no purgatory, no ceasing to exist. At death, the soul goes immediately into conscious existence, the believer to be with Christ (Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8), the unbeliever to punishment (Luke 16:22–26); at Christ’s return, all will be raised and judged (John 5:28–29; Revelation 20:11–15).

So Christ, having been offered once to bear the sins of many. Key words. “Offered once” (hapax prosenechtheis). Christ’s death corresponds to the one death of every person; but his death was for others. “To bear the sins” (anenenkein hamartias, carry up sins), echoing Isaiah 53:12 (“he bore the sin of many”). He carried our sins, bearing their penalty (1 Peter 2:24). “Many” (pollōn): Isaiah’s word, also used by Jesus (Mark 10:45). The “many” are those for whom he died, the many sons brought to glory (2:10).

Will appear a second time. Key words. “Appear” (ophthēsetai, will be seen). Christ’s second coming will be visible. On the Day of Atonement, the people waited outside while the high priest was in the Most Holy Place; when he came out, they knew the sacrifice had been accepted. So Christ will come out from heaven, to the joy of his people.

Not to deal with sin. Key words. Literally “without sin” (chōris hamartias): not to bear sin again. His dealing with sin was finished at his first coming.

But to save those who are eagerly waiting for him. Key words. “Save” (eis sōtērian, for salvation): the final, full salvation of his people, including the resurrection of their bodies (Romans 8:23; Philippians 3:20–21). “Eagerly waiting” (apekdechomenois, waiting with eager expectation): a mark of true believers (Titus 2:13; 2 Timothy 4:8).

Where Christians differ: is there a second chance after death, or a purgatory? Some teach that those who never heard the gospel will have an opportunity after death; Roman Catholic teaching holds that many believers pass through purgatory to be purified before heaven. Others teach soul sleep (unconsciousness until resurrection) or annihilation. Verdict: This verse is clear: death, then judgement. Our eternal destiny is fixed at death (Luke 16:26). Believers enter conscious joy with Christ immediately (Luke 23:43; Philippians 1:23); there is no purgatory, because Christ’s once-for-all sacrifice fully cleanses (10:14). Unbelievers face conscious punishment, eternal and real (Matthew 25:46; Revelation 14:11). The time to respond to the gospel is now (3:13; 2 Corinthians 6:2).

What it does not mean. “Appear a second time” does not mean there will be a secret coming before his visible return. Scripture speaks of one future return, visible and glorious, at which he gathers his people and judges the world (Matthew 24:30–31; 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–10).

In a sentence. Just as everyone is destined to die once and after that to face judgement, so Christ was offered once to carry the sins of many, and he will appear a second time, not to deal with sin, but to bring salvation to those who are eagerly waiting for him.

For worship. Are you eagerly waiting for Christ? Pray today for his return, and live as one ready to meet him.

parallels.desc: he bore the sin of many

10.title: Once for All: The New and Living Way
10.overview:
Chapter 10 is the summit of the letter’s central argument. Priesthood (chapters 5–7), covenant (8) and sacrifice (9) converge here. The law’s yearly animal sacrifices are set against Christ’s single offering, with Psalm 40 as the key: “I have come to do your will, O God.” By that will, through the offering of his body once for all, “we have been sanctified.”

Then the longest application (vv. 19–39): draw near to God, hold fast the confession, and stir one another up to love and good works. The fourth and severest warning follows (vv. 26–31), balanced at once by encouragement: remember how you once joyfully accepted the loss of your property. You need endurance for a little while more. The coming one will come.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — One Sacrifice, and a Priest Who Sat Down
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The writer explains why the old sacrifices could never deal with sin. The law was only a shadow of the good things to come, not the reality, so its sacrifices, repeated year after year, could not make worshippers complete; their repetition was itself a yearly reminder of sin, since animal blood cannot remove it. Psalm 40 shows what replaces them: Christ came to do God’s will in the body prepared for him, setting aside the old system. By that will we have been made holy through the once-for-all offering of his body. The old priests stood daily, repeating sacrifices; Christ offered one sacrifice for all time and sat down at God’s right hand, waiting for his enemies to be subdued. The Spirit’s promise of the new covenant in Jeremiah confirms it: God will remember sins no more, and where sins are forgiven no further offering is needed.
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Tenses in One Sentence

By a single offering Christ has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified. Where sins are forgiven, there is no longer any offering for sin.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The yearly sacrifices were a reminder of sins, and their repetition confessed that they had not finished the work.

Now: Standing before God does not wait on our progress; our progress flows from a finished offering.

verseByVerse.quote: For since the law has but a shadow of the good things to come instead of the true form of these realities, it can never, by the same sacrifices that are continually offered every year, make perfect those who draw near. Otherwise, would they not have ceased to be offered, since the worshipers, having once been cleansed, would no longer have any consciousness of sins?
verseByVerse.commentary:
For since the law has but a shadow of the good things to come instead of the true form of these realities, it can never, by the same sacrifices that are continually offered every year, make perfect those who draw near. Otherwise, would they not have ceased to be offered, since the worshipers, having once been cleansed, would no longer have any consciousness of sins?

Meaning first. Hebrews 10 completes the great argument about Christ’s sacrifice and then turns it into urgent appeal. First, the old sacrifices could never perfect worshippers; their endless repetition proved it, reminding people of sins every year, since animal blood cannot take sins away (vv. 1–4). Christ came, as Psalm 40 foretold, not to offer more animals but to do God’s will in the body prepared for him, and by that will we have been sanctified through the offering of his body once for all (vv. 5–10). The old priests stood daily offering sacrifices that could never remove sin; Christ offered one sacrifice for all time and sat down, for by that single offering he has perfected forever those being made holy, as the Spirit testifies in Jeremiah’s promise that God will remember sins no more; where there is forgiveness, no more offering is needed (vv. 11–18). Then the appeal (vv. 19–25): since we have confidence to enter God’s presence by Jesus’ blood through the new and living way he opened, let us draw near with sincere hearts, hold fast our hope, and stir one another to love and good works, not giving up meeting together. Then the fourth warning (vv. 26–31): for those who deliberately go on sinning after knowing the truth, trampling the Son of God and insulting the Spirit of grace, no sacrifice remains, only fearful judgement. Finally, encouragement (vv. 32–39): remember how you endured persecution and joyfully accepted the loss of property; do not throw away your confidence; you need endurance; the coming one will come soon; we are not those who shrink back and are destroyed, but those who believe and are saved.

For since the law has but a shadow of the good things to come. Key words. “Shadow” (skian), as in 8:5. A shadow shows the outline of something real but is not the thing itself. “Good things to come”: the blessings of the new covenant in Christ (9:11).

Instead of the true form of these realities. Key words. “True form” (eikona, image, actual likeness, the very substance). The law had a shadow, not the reality. Christ is the substance (Colossians 2:17).

It can never, by the same sacrifices that are continually offered every year, make perfect those who draw near. Key words. “Never” (oudepote). “Continually” (eis to diēnekes, perpetually). “Every year”: the Day of Atonement. “Make perfect” (teleiōsai), as in 7:19 and 9:9: bring to full cleansing and access.

Otherwise, would they not have ceased to be offered? Key words. The logical argument: if the sacrifices really worked, they would have stopped. A medicine that cures is not taken forever.

Since the worshipers, having once been cleansed, would no longer have any consciousness of sins. Key words. “Once been cleansed” (hapax kekatharismenous, cleansed once for all). “Consciousness of sins” (syneidēsin hamartiōn, conscience of sins, sense of guilt). If truly cleansed, they would no longer carry guilt. Not that they would never be aware of sinning, but that they would no longer bear the burden of unremoved guilt before God.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the old sacrifices were useless or that God did not command them. They were God’s appointed shadows, pointing to Christ. But they could not achieve what only Christ’s sacrifice could.

In a sentence. The law is only a shadow of the good things that were coming, not the realities themselves. That is why it can never, by the same sacrifices repeated endlessly year after year, make perfect those who come near to worship. If it could, would the sacrifices not have stopped being offered? The worshippers would have been cleansed once for all and would no longer have felt guilty for their sins.

For worship. If you still carry guilt for forgiven sins, hear this: Christ has cleansed you once for all. Let your conscience rest in him.

verseByVerse.quote: But in these sacrifices there is a reminder of sins every year. For it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But in these sacrifices there is a reminder of sins every year. For it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins.

But in these sacrifices there is a reminder of sins every year. Key words. “Reminder” (anamnēsis, remembrance, recollection). Instead of removing sins, the annual sacrifices reminded people of them. Each Day of Atonement said: your sins are still there. Contrast the new covenant, where God remembers sins no more (8:12; 10:17). Interestingly, Jesus uses the same word, anamnēsis, of the Lord’s Supper (“do this in remembrance of me,” Luke 22:19). The old ritual remembered sins; the new remembers the Saviour who removed them.

For it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins. Key words. “Impossible” (adynaton), the same strong word as 6:4, 18. “Take away” (aphairein, remove, lift off). An animal cannot substitute for a human being; it is not of the same nature, nor can it willingly offer itself, nor is it of infinite worth. The old sacrifices could cleanse ritually, and pointed to Christ, but they could not remove guilt before God. Only the sacrifice of a sinless man who is also God could do that.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Old Testament believers were not truly forgiven. They were forgiven through faith in God’s promise, and the sacrifices were the means God appointed for that faith, but the forgiveness was grounded in Christ’s future sacrifice (9:15; Romans 3:25).

In a sentence. Instead, those sacrifices are an annual reminder of sins, because it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take sins away.

For worship. At the Lord’s Table, remember not your sins, but your Saviour, who took them away.

verseByVerse.quote: Consequently, when Christ came into the world, he said, “Sacrifices and offerings you have not desired, but a body have you prepared for me; in burnt offerings and sin offerings you have taken no pleasure. Then I said, ’Behold, I have come to do your will, O God, as it is written of me in the scroll of the book.’”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Consequently, when Christ came into the world, he said, “Sacrifices and offerings you have not desired, but a body have you prepared for me; in burnt offerings and sin offerings you have taken no pleasure. Then I said, ‘Behold, I have come to do your will, O God, as it is written of me in the scroll of the book.’”

Consequently, when Christ came into the world, he said. Key words. “Came into the world” (eiserchomenos eis ton kosmon): his incarnation. The words of Psalm 40:6–8 are presented as the words of Christ himself, spoken to the Father as he entered the world. David wrote them, but they find their full meaning in the Son.

Sacrifices and offerings you have not desired. Key words. “Sacrifices” (thysian, animal sacrifices) and “offerings” (prosphoran, grain offerings). God did not desire them for their own sake. What he desired was obedience from the heart (1 Samuel 15:22; Psalm 51:16–17; Hosea 6:6; Micah 6:6–8).

But a body have you prepared for me. Key words. “A body have you prepared for me” follows the Greek Old Testament; the Hebrew reads “you have opened my ears” (literally “ears you have dug for me”), meaning God gave the ability to hear and obey. The Greek translators interpreted it as a reference to the whole body, of which the ears are part: God prepared a whole person for obedience. Under the Spirit’s guidance, the author uses the Greek version because it points precisely to the incarnation: the Father prepared a human body for the Son, in which he could obey perfectly and offer himself as the sacrifice (v. 10).
