The Lord is my helper; I will not fear; what can man do to me? Key words. From Psalm 118:6. “Helper” (boēthos, one who runs to help at a cry), as in 2:18. If God is for us, human enemies, persecutors and losses cannot finally harm us (Romans 8:31; Matthew 10:28).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should never work to provide or save. Diligence and provision are biblical (1 Timothy 5:8). It means our security and contentment rest in God, not in money.

In a sentence. Do not let love of money rule your lives; be satisfied with what you have, because God himself has said, “I will never leave you; I will never abandon you.” So we can say with confidence, “The Lord is my helper; I will not be afraid. What can mere people do to me?”

For worship. Repeat God’s promise to yourself today: “I will never leave you nor forsake you.” Let it cure your anxiety about money.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: They should remember the leaders who taught them God’s word, consider the outcome of their lives and imitate their faith, for Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today and for ever. They must not be carried away by strange teachings, especially about ritual foods; the heart is strengthened by grace. Christians have an altar from which the old priesthood has no right to eat. Just as the bodies of sacrificial animals were burned outside the camp, Jesus suffered outside the city gate to make his people holy by his blood. So believers should go out to him outside the camp, bearing the disgrace he bore, because here they have no lasting city but seek the one to come. Through him they are to offer God a continual sacrifice of praise and not neglect to do good and share, which pleases God. They should obey and submit to their leaders, who keep watch over their souls and must give account, so that their work is a joy and not a burden. And they should pray for the writer, who has a clear conscience and hopes to be restored to them soon.
verseByVerse.theology:
Outside the Camp

Jesus suffered outside the gate, as the sin offering was burned outside the camp. Go to him there, bearing his reproach, and offer the sacrifices that please God: praise, doing good and sharing.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: For these readers the camp was home — temple, synagogue, festivals and family table.

Now: Leaving what is not lasting is not homelessness; it is going to where he is.

verseByVerse.quote: Remember your leaders, those who spoke to you the word of God. Consider the outcome of their way of life, and imitate their faith. Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remember your leaders, those who spoke to you the word of God. Consider the outcome of their way of life, and imitate their faith. Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.

Remember your leaders, those who spoke to you the word of God. Key words. “Leaders” (hēgoumenōn, those who lead, guide). Probably the founding leaders of the church, perhaps including apostles, who first preached the gospel to them (2:3) and had since died. “Spoke the word of God”: their authority was the word they preached.

Consider the outcome of their way of life. Key words. “Consider” (anatheōrountes, look carefully at, observe closely). “Outcome” (ekbasin, end, result, exit): how their lives ended. Perhaps some died as martyrs, others in faith. They finished well.

And imitate their faith. Key words. “Imitate” (mimeisthe), as in 6:12. Not their personalities or methods, but their faith.

Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever. Key words. “The same” (ho autos), echoing 1:12. Leaders come and go, but Jesus remains. The same Christ who sustained their former leaders will sustain them. Yesterday: in his earthly life and ministry, and in the faith of their leaders. Today: interceding for them now (7:25). Forever: unchanging in his person, promises and power. This also prepares for verse 9: since Christ does not change, there is no need for new, strange teachings.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ is static or inactive. He acts in every generation. It means his character, promises and saving work do not change.

In a sentence. Remember your leaders, who spoke the word of God to you. Think about how their lives turned out, and imitate their faith. Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today and for ever.

For worship. Thank God for those who first taught you the gospel. And rest in the unchanging Christ, who was faithful to them and will be faithful to you.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be led away by diverse and strange teachings, for it is good for the heart to be strengthened by grace, not by foods, which have not benefited those devoted to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be led away by diverse and strange teachings, for it is good for the heart to be strengthened by grace, not by foods, which have not benefited those devoted to them.

Do not be led away by diverse and strange teachings. Key words. “Led away” (parapheresthe, carried aside, swept off course), like a ship drifting (2:1). “Diverse” (poikilais, varied, many-coloured). “Strange” (xenais, foreign, alien to the gospel). Since Christ does not change (v. 8), new teachings that depart from him should be rejected.

For it is good for the heart to be strengthened by grace. Key words. “Strengthened” (bebaiousthai, made firm, established). “By grace” (chariti): by God’s free favour in Christ. The heart is established by grace, received through the gospel, not by rituals.

Not by foods. Key words. “Foods” (brōmasin): probably Jewish food laws, sacrificial meals, or special ritual meals that some taught were necessary for spiritual strength. The old covenant sacrificial meals (where worshippers ate part of the offerings) may be in view, given verse 10.

Which have not benefited those devoted to them. Key words. “Devoted to them” (hoi peripatountes, those who walk in them, live by them). Such practices never truly strengthened anyone spiritually (9:9–10; Colossians 2:16–23).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should be indifferent to what they eat for health. It means food rules do not make us right with God or spiritually strong (Romans 14:17; 1 Corinthians 8:8).

In a sentence. Do not be carried off course by all kinds of strange teachings. It is good for our hearts to be strengthened by grace, not by rules about food, which are of no value to those who observe them.

On a Tuesday. Be wary of teachings that offer spiritual strength through rules and rituals rather than through grace. Feed your heart on the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: We have an altar from which those who serve the tent have no right to eat. For the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the holy places by the high priest as a sacrifice for sin are burned outside the camp. So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We have an altar from which those who serve the tent have no right to eat. For the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the holy places by the high priest as a sacrifice for sin are burned outside the camp. So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood.

We have an altar. Key words. “Altar” (thysiastērion, place of sacrifice). The Christian altar is the cross, or Christ’s sacrifice itself. We “eat” from it by faith, feeding spiritually on Christ crucified (John 6:53–58).

From which those who serve the tent have no right to eat. Key words. “Those who serve the tent”: those who cling to the old tabernacle worship. “No right” (ouk echousin exousian, no authority). Under the old covenant, priests ate portions of many sacrifices, but never of the Day of Atonement sin offering, which was wholly burned (Leviticus 6:30; 16:27). Christ is the true sin offering; those who stay with the old system cannot share in him.

For the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the holy places by the high priest as a sacrifice for sin are burned outside the camp. Key words. On the Day of Atonement, the blood of the bull and goat was brought into the Most Holy Place, and their bodies were burned outside the camp (Leviticus 16:27).

So Jesus also suffered outside the gate. Key words. “Outside the gate”: Jesus was crucified outside the walls of Jerusalem (John 19:17, 20; Matthew 27:32). Like the sin offering, he was put outside, rejected, treated as unclean. Outside the camp was the place of the unclean, the leper, the outcast (Leviticus 13:46; Numbers 15:35–36).

In order to sanctify the people through his own blood. Key words. “Sanctify” (hagiasē, make holy), as in 10:10, 14. “The people” (ton laon): his people. Through his rejection and death, he made his people holy.

Where Christians differ: is the Lord’s Table an altar? Roman Catholic and some Anglo-Catholic traditions identify this altar with the communion table, on which the sacrifice of the Mass is offered. Verdict: The New Testament never calls the Lord’s Table an altar. The altar here is Christ’s once-for-all sacrifice on the cross (7:27; 10:10–14). We “eat” from it by faith in his finished work, especially as we receive the Lord’s Supper, where Christ is spiritually present and we feed on him by faith; but there is no new sacrifice offered.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should despise Jewish people. The point is that the old covenant system cannot give access to Christ’s benefits; only faith in him can.

In a sentence. We have an altar from which those who minister at the tabernacle have no right to eat. The high priest carries the blood of animals into the Most Holy Place as a sin offering, but their bodies are burned outside the camp. In the same way, Jesus suffered outside the city gate to make the people holy through his own blood.

For worship. Thank Jesus that he went outside the gate, rejected and shamed, to make you holy. Feed on him by faith today.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore let us go to him outside the camp and bear the reproach he endured. For here we have no lasting city, but we seek the city that is to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore let us go to him outside the camp and bear the reproach he endured. For here we have no lasting city, but we seek the city that is to come.

Therefore let us go to him outside the camp. Key words. “Go” (exerchōmetha, go out, keep going out). “Outside the camp”: for the readers, this meant leaving behind the security and respectability of Judaism, its temple, its rituals and its community, to identify fully with the rejected Christ. Following Jesus means going where he went.

And bear the reproach he endured. Key words. “Reproach” (oneidismon, disgrace, insult), as of Moses in 11:26. Identifying with Christ brings shame from those who reject him. The readers were tempted to avoid it by returning to Judaism. They must embrace it.

For here we have no lasting city. Key words. “Lasting” (menousan, abiding, permanent). Jerusalem itself, the holy city, was not permanent; it would be destroyed in AD 70. No earthly city, nation or institution is our permanent home.

But we seek the city that is to come. Key words. “Seek” (epizētoumen, search for, long for). The heavenly Jerusalem (11:10, 16; 12:22). Like Abraham, we are pilgrims.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should withdraw from society or not care about their earthly cities. We are to seek the welfare of the city where we live (Jeremiah 29:7). But we do not put our ultimate hope there.

In a sentence. So let us go out to him outside the camp, carrying the disgrace he bore. For here we do not have a permanent city; we are looking for the city that is coming.

On a Tuesday. Where does following Jesus mean going “outside the camp” for you: risking reputation, comfort or acceptance? Go to him there.

verseByVerse.quote: Through him then let us continually offer up a sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips that acknowledge his name. Do not neglect to do good and to share what you have, for such sacrifices are pleasing to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Through him then let us continually offer up a sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips that acknowledge his name. Do not neglect to do good and to share what you have, for such sacrifices are pleasing to God.

Through him then let us continually offer up a sacrifice of praise to God. Key words. “Through him” (di’ autou): through Christ, our High Priest. Our offerings are acceptable only through him (1 Peter 2:5). “Continually” (dia pantos), as the old priests offered continually (9:6); our praise never stops. “Sacrifice of praise” (thysian aineseōs): the Old Testament thank offering (Leviticus 7:12; Psalm 50:14, 23; 116:17). No more sacrifices for sin are needed (10:18), but thank offerings continue.

That is, the fruit of lips that acknowledge his name. Key words. “Fruit of lips” (karpon cheileōn), from Hosea 14:2 (Greek). “Acknowledge” (homologountōn, confess, profess). Praising God and confessing Christ openly, the very thing the readers were tempted to stop doing.

Do not neglect to do good and to share what you have. Key words. “Do good” (eupoiias, doing good, kindness). “Share” (koinōnias, fellowship, generosity, sharing possessions). Practical generosity.

For such sacrifices are pleasing to God. Key words. “Pleasing” (euaresteitai), as in 11:5–6. Two kinds of Christian sacrifice: praise (Godward) and good works (manward). Both are worship (Romans 12:1; Philippians 4:18).

What it does not mean. It does not mean these sacrifices atone for sin. They are responses of gratitude to Christ’s completed atonement.

In a sentence. Through Jesus, therefore, let us keep offering God a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that openly confess his name. And do not forget to do good and to share with others, for with such sacrifices God is pleased.

For worship. Offer God two sacrifices today: praise from your lips and a generous act for someone in need.

verseByVerse.quote: Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they are keeping watch over your souls, as those who will have to give an account. Let them do this with joy and not with groaning, for that would be of no advantage to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they are keeping watch over your souls, as those who will have to give an account. Let them do this with joy and not with groaning, for that would be of no advantage to you.

Obey your leaders and submit to them. Key words. “Leaders” (hēgoumenois): their present leaders, in contrast with the former ones (v. 7). “Obey” (peithesthe, be persuaded by, follow). “Submit” (hypeikete, yield, defer). In a time of temptation and false teaching, the church must follow its faithful leaders, the elders who teach God’s word.

For they are keeping watch over your souls. Key words. “Keeping watch” (agrypnousin, staying awake, losing sleep, being vigilant), like a shepherd watching the flock at night (Luke 2:8) or a sentry on guard. Faithful elders lose sleep over their people.

As those who will have to give an account. Key words. “Give an account” (logon apodōsontes). Leaders will answer to God for how they cared for their people (James 3:1; Ezekiel 34; 1 Peter 5:1–4). This makes their task serious and their authority accountable.

Let them do this with joy and not with groaning. Key words. “Groaning” (stenazontes, sighing, grieving). Leaders can serve joyfully or with grief, depending partly on how the people respond.

For that would be of no advantage to you. Key words. “Of no advantage” (alysiteles, unprofitable, harmful). A church that makes its leaders groan harms itself.

What it does not mean. It does not mean blind obedience to leaders who teach error or command sin (Acts 5:29; Galatians 1:8–9). It means willing, respectful following of leaders who faithfully teach God’s word and care for the flock. Nor does it support a single ruling bishop; “leaders” is plural, consistent with a plurality of elders.

In a sentence. Have confidence in your leaders and follow their guidance, because they keep watch over you as people who must give an account. Let them do this with joy, not with sighs of grief, for that would do you no good.

On a Tuesday. How can you make your elders’ work a joy this week? Encourage them, pray for them, and follow their faithful guidance.

verseByVerse.quote: Pray for us, for we are sure that we have a clear conscience, desiring to act honorably in all things. I urge you the more earnestly to do this in order that I may be restored to you the sooner.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pray for us, for we are sure that we have a clear conscience, desiring to act honorably in all things. I urge you the more earnestly to do this in order that I may be restored to you the sooner.

Pray for us. Key words. “Pray” (proseuchesthe, keep praying). “Us”: the author and his companions. Every leader needs the prayers of God’s people.

For we are sure that we have a clear conscience. Key words. “Sure” (peithometha, are persuaded). “Clear conscience” (kalēn syneidēsin, good conscience). Perhaps the author had been criticised. He is confident that his motives and conduct are right.

Desiring to act honorably in all things. Key words. “Honorably” (kalōs, well, rightly, nobly). His goal is integrity in everything.

I urge you the more earnestly to do this in order that I may be restored to you the sooner. Key words. “Restored” (apokatastathō, given back). The author had been with them before and was now separated, perhaps by imprisonment or other circumstances. He believes their prayers will make a real difference.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the author claimed sinlessness. A clear conscience means not knowingly living in hypocrisy or unconfessed sin.

In a sentence. Pray for us. We are sure that our conscience is clear, and we want to live honourably in every way. I especially urge you to pray so that I may be returned to you soon.

On a Tuesday. Pray today, by name, for your pastor and for a missionary you know. Your prayers matter.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The letter closes with a prayer of blessing. The writer asks that the God of peace, who raised our Lord Jesus from the dead, the great shepherd of his flock, through the blood that seals the everlasting covenant, will supply them with every good thing they need to do his will, and will himself produce in them what pleases him, through Jesus Christ, to whom glory belongs for ever. He asks them to take his short message of encouragement patiently, tells them Timothy has been set free and may travel with him, sends greetings to their leaders and to all God’s people, including from believers from Italy, and ends with grace.
verseByVerse.theology:
The God Who Works in Us

The God of peace, who brought again from the dead the great shepherd of the sheep, equips his people and works in them what pleases him. What he requires, he supplies.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The writer calls his letter a “word of exhortation”, a sermon sent to people he knows and misses.

Now: After its hardest warnings, the letter ends with grace for all.

verseByVerse.quote: Now may the God of peace who brought again from the dead our Lord Jesus, the great shepherd of the sheep, by the blood of the eternal covenant, equip you with everything good that you may do his will, working in us that which is pleasing in his sight, through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now may the God of peace who brought again from the dead our Lord Jesus, the great shepherd of the sheep, by the blood of the eternal covenant, equip you with everything good that you may do his will, working in us that which is pleasing in his sight, through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

Now may the God of peace. Key words. “God of peace” (ho theos tēs eirēnēs): the God who has made peace with sinners through Christ’s blood, and who gives peace (Romans 15:33; 16:20; 1 Thessalonians 5:23). Fitting for a church troubled by persecution and tempted toward division.

Who brought again from the dead our Lord Jesus. Key words. “Brought again” (anagagōn, led up, brought back). The only explicit mention of the resurrection in Hebrews, though it is assumed throughout (his indestructible life, 7:16; his entry into heaven).

The great shepherd of the sheep. Key words. “Great shepherd” (ton poimena tōn probatōn ton megan). Echoing Isaiah 63:11, where God brought up from the sea the shepherd of his flock (Moses). Jesus is the greater shepherd (John 10:11, 14; 1 Peter 2:25; 5:4), who laid down his life for the sheep and was brought back from death.

By the blood of the eternal covenant. Key words. “Eternal covenant” (diathēkēs aiōniou): the new covenant, which will never be replaced (Isaiah 55:3; Jeremiah 32:40; Ezekiel 37:26). Christ’s blood ratified it; God raised him because his sacrifice was accepted. The resurrection is the Father’s seal on the covenant.

Equip you with everything good that you may do his will. Key words. “Equip” (katartisai, make complete, fit out, mend, restore, as nets are mended). “Do his will”: as Christ came to do God’s will (10:7, 9), so his people do it by his equipping.

Working in us that which is pleasing in his sight. Key words. “Working” (poiōn, doing, producing). God himself works in us what pleases him (Philippians 2:13). Our obedience is real, but it is God’s work in us.

Through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen. Key words. “To whom”: probably Christ, though possibly God the Father. Either way, glory is given to God through Christ. The letter that exalts Christ above angels, Moses and Aaron ends by giving him eternal glory.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we are passive. God equips us so that we do his will. Divine work and human obedience go together.

In a sentence. Now may the God of peace, who through the blood of the eternal covenant brought back from the dead our Lord Jesus, that great Shepherd of the sheep, equip you with everything good for doing his will, and may he work in us what is pleasing to him, through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen.

For worship. Pray this benediction over yourself and your church today. Ask the God of peace to equip you for his will.

verseByVerse.quote: I appeal to you, brothers, bear with my word of exhortation, for I have written to you briefly. You should know that our brother Timothy has been released, with whom I shall see you if he comes soon. Greet all your leaders and all the saints. Those who come from Italy send you greetings. Grace be with all of you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I appeal to you, brothers, bear with my word of exhortation, for I have written to you briefly. You should know that our brother Timothy has been released, with whom I shall see you if he comes soon. Greet all your leaders and all the saints. Those who come from Italy send you greetings. Grace be with all of you.

I appeal to you, brothers, bear with my word of exhortation. Key words. “Bear with” (anechesthe, put up with, listen patiently). The warnings have been severe; the author asks them to receive them in good spirit. “Word of exhortation” (tou logou tēs paraklēseōs): a phrase used of a synagogue sermon (Acts 13:15). Hebrews is essentially a written sermon.

For I have written to you briefly. Key words. “Briefly” (dia bracheōn). Hebrews takes under an hour to read aloud; given the vastness of its subject, it is brief (9:5; 11:32).

You should know that our brother Timothy has been released. Key words. Timothy had evidently been in prison. “Released” (apolelymenon, set free). This is the only mention of Timothy’s imprisonment in the New Testament, perhaps after Paul’s death in Rome.

With whom I shall see you if he comes soon. Key words. The author planned to travel with Timothy to visit the readers.

Greet all your leaders and all the saints. Key words. “All your leaders”: plural, the elders (v. 17). “All the saints”: every believer, holy in Christ.

Those who come from Italy send you greetings. Key words. “Those who come from Italy” (hoi apo tēs Italias) can mean Italians living abroad, sending greetings home to Rome, or people in Italy sending greetings elsewhere. The first reading suggests the letter was sent to Rome, which fits other evidence: the earliest known use of Hebrews was by Clement of Rome, around AD 95.

Grace be with all of you. Key words. The last word of the letter: grace. The letter has warned, exhorted and taught, but all rests on grace (4:16; 12:15; 13:9).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the letter’s warnings were overstated. The author asks them to bear with his exhortation precisely because it was serious, and loving.

In a sentence. Brothers and sisters, I urge you to listen patiently to my message of encouragement, for I have written to you only briefly. I want you to know that our brother Timothy has been released. If he arrives soon, I will come with him to see you. Greet all your leaders and all God’s people. Those from Italy send you their greetings. Grace be with you all.

For worship. Thank God for the whole letter to the Hebrews: Christ is better, and his grace is with you all.
verseByVerse.note: Timothy had evidently been in prison. “Those who come from Italy” may be Italians abroad sending greetings home, or believers in Italy itself.

13.text: <sup>1</sup>Let brotherly love continue.<sup>2</sup>Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.<sup>3</sup>Remember those who are in prison, as though in prison with them, and those who are mistreated, since you also are in the body.<sup>4</sup>Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the marriage bed be undefiled, for God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterous.<sup>5</sup>Keep your life free from love of money, and be content with what you have, for he has said, “I will never leave you nor forsake you.”<sup>6</sup>So we can confidently say, “The Lord is my helper; I will not fear; what can man do to me?”<sup>7</sup>Remember your leaders, those who spoke to you the word of God. Consider the outcome of their way of life, and imitate their faith.<sup>8</sup>Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.<sup>9</sup>Do not be led away by diverse and strange teachings, for it is good for the heart to be strengthened by grace, not by foods, which have not benefited those devoted to them.<sup>10</sup>We have an altar from which those who serve the tent have no right to eat.<sup>11</sup>For the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the holy places by the high priest as a sacrifice for sin are burned outside the camp.<sup>12</sup>So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood.<sup>13</sup>Therefore let us go to him outside the camp and bear the reproach he endured.<sup>14</sup>For here we have no lasting city, but we seek the city that is to come.<sup>15</sup>Through him then let us continually offer up a sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips that acknowledge his name.<sup>16</sup>Do not neglect to do good and to share what you have, for such sacrifices are pleasing to God.<sup>17</sup>Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they are keeping watch over your souls, as those who will have to give an account. Let them do this with joy and not with groaning, for that would be of no advantage to you.<sup>18</sup>Pray for us, for we are sure that we have a clear conscience, desiring to act honorably in all things.<sup>19</sup>I urge you the more earnestly to do this in order that I may be restored to you the sooner.<sup>20</sup>Now may the God of peace who brought again from the dead our Lord Jesus, the great shepherd of the sheep, by the blood of the eternal covenant,<sup>21</sup>equip you with everything good that you may do his will, working in us that which is pleasing in his sight, through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.<sup>22</sup>I appeal to you, brothers, bear with my word of exhortation, for I have written to you briefly.<sup>23</sup>You should know that our brother Timothy has been released, with whom I shall see you if he comes soon.<sup>24</sup>Greet all your leaders and all the saints. Those who come from Italy send you greetings.<sup>25</sup>Grace be with all of you.
